📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Eurovision Song Contest crowned its first Asia champion in Bangkok on Saturday, in an event that tested whether a high-camp singing competition with an ardent fan base could appeal to audiences in a newly introduced market.

Sources indicate that carmelle of the Philippines was declared the winner of the inaugural Eurovision Song Contest Asia, beating out artists and original songs from 10 other countries: Bangladesh, Bhutan, Cambodia, Laos, Malaysia, Mongolia, Nepal, South Korea, Thailand and Vietnam. The show was live-streamed on YouTube and broadcast by television stations across the region.

Eurovision has been a fixture of the European cultural calendar since it began in 1956. Past winners include Sweden’s ABBA and the Canadian chanteuse Celine Dion, who represented Switzerland in 1988.

In a recent development, asian artists have readily embraced the kitschy outfits and spectacular sets that are part of Eurovision tradition, with costumes that include traditional dress, as well as feathered capes and sequined corsets. Malaysia’s performer plans to enter the stage in a giant teardrop.

But the Eurovision format has not been tested in Asia. Fans and regional partners have expressed concern in recent weeks that budget constraints, production issues and weak audience demand could imperil the spinoff. Organizers say the contest could take time to build an audience.

Sources indicate that “It would be profoundly arrogant to think that just because we have a heritage brand and a huge global audience for the European show, that we would walk in and demand it to be the same here,” mentioned Martin Green, the European Broadcasting Union’s director of the Eurovision Song Contest. “Like any latest thing, it needs to find its roots.”.

In a recent development, two previous attempts to take the competition to Asia were abandoned by the European Broadcasting Union, which owns Eurovision, and its partners in the region. A Eurovision spinoff in the United States, NBC’s American Song Contest, ran for one season in 2022.

Sources indicate that the Asian edition kicking off on Saturday is far smaller than its European counterpart. Eurovision organizers said they were in talks with more countries to join future seasons. They include China, Japan and India, whose music industries have global reach.

Recent findings suggest that “Bringing the world together through music is a fundamentally good idea,” Mr. Green remarked. “Europe shouldn’t keep it to itself.”.

Industry observers note that ballads: Nine of the competition’s 11 participating countries picked performers singing about love in a wide range of styles, from ballads to a cappella hip-hop. Their choices suggest that the bombastic music often associated with victors of the European edition might not be a winning formula for Asian viewers. Read more ›.

Sources indicate that fans: Our reporter spoke to some of the fans who traveled to Bangkok for Eurovision. Read more ›.

Politics: Geopolitics have long intruded on the European edition of the Eurovision Song Contest, but they were not really a factor as the event prepared to expand into Asia. Read more ›.

Industry observers note that no demonstrates: For a competition meant to introduce the diversity of Asian pop music to the world, the lineup for the first Eurovision Song Contest Asia has several notable absences, starting with China and India. Read more ›.

Recent findings suggest that as Thailand’s Mang and Daou waited to learn whether they had won, the 26-year-old Mang was shown onscreen crying as if she couldn’t take the tension. That’s the sort of emotion needed to make Eurovision’s expansion into Asia a success. Acts have to want the title. But the show will also need the massive Asian nations -- India, Japan and China -- to buy in, and much could now depend on the reaction in the Philippines to Carmelle’s win. The event was far less spectacular than a typical Eurovision in Europe. It also featured far too many ballads for my taste, but it was a fun afternoon’s viewing.

Shiesam Flores, 27, a clerk from the eastern region of Bicol in the Philippines, has been watching the show at a party with her friends — and hoping that Carmelle would prevail.

It has been revealed that “It was nerve-wracking, nail biting suspense!” she mentioned. “But we know she would win! What a talent!”.

The Philippines’ Carmelle wins the first Eurovision Song Contest Asia, pushing Thailand’s Mang and Daou into second.

The crowd roared in disappointment as Malaysia got only 70 points from the public vote.

Thailand takes a massive lead thanks to the public vote, but the genius of this voting process is we won’t know whether the Philippines can overcome them until the last seconds.

In a recent development, the public gave Beatmosphere, from Bangladesh, just 19 points. They looked surprisingly happy after getting such a low total, and it’s now confirmed they’ve come in a distant last.

Dara has brought the Eurovision Asia trophy to the stage. It’s a sparkly gold microphone.

The public vote can be brutal, as some acts rapidly learn that few viewers liked them.

The jury votes are all in, and it’s close. The Philippines is first with 93 points, Vietnam second with 83 points and Malaysia third with 82 points. We’re about to learn how many points each country’s act received from the public, starting with the current last place act, Bangladesh’s beatboxing-heavy crew Beatmosphere. It has 16 points.

Industry observers note that one of the best parts of Eurovision is how the public’s choice is often completely diffferent from those of the juries, so don’t worry if your favorite act isn’t top of the ranking after the jury votes are all in. The Philippine’s jury, the first we’ve heard from, just gave its 12 points to Malaysia. That doesn’t mean it’ll win.

Fans are decked out in flags and sequins for the first-ever Asia Eurovision here in Bangkok.

The problem Eurovision has with interval acts like Jeff Satur is that their stagecraft, singing ability and melodies are often a million times better than the artists in competition. Satur, who has 1.4 million monthly listeners on Spotify and over five million Instagram fans, has dozens of camp dancers onstage and a statue of a dragon. He would have cruised to victory if he’d been in competition, especially because of his ability to hold high notes close to the range only dogs can hear.

Simon Robinson, one of the fans who traveled to Bangkok for the Eurovision Song Contest on Saturday, said that his history with the competition is nearly as long as its seven-decade run.

He was eight years old when he first watched it with his family in Yorkshire, England, when Britain's Mary Hopkin finished in second place behind Ireland’s Dana.

Sources indicate that “I really liked the concept of bringing Europe together after the war,” said Mr. Robinson, 63, who now lives in Melbourne, Australia. He described the contest’s annual broadcast as a social activity for his family and neighbors.

“Eurovision helped to create the European identity,” he added.

Other fans had their own motivations for traveling to see the contest’s first Asian edition.

Some are Europeans living in Asia, on the hunt for nostalgia, while others are Americans who were eager to experience their first Eurovision.

Lee Hudson, an American television executive based in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, said that he gets emotional when he talks about Eurovision, which he has watched since 2012.

Recent findings suggest that “The only reason I know any music from European countries is because I heard them on Eurovision,” he noted. “Eurovision Asia makes sense because the musical cultures are distinct.”.

Recent findings suggest that mr. Hudson remarked he still listens to Loreen’s “Euphoria,” which won the competition for Sweden in 2012.

It was also the first Eurovision that Drew Andrea watched from his home in Sydney. A year later, he got a passport to fly to Sweden for the 2013 edition, and has attended every final since. Coming to Bangkok for Eurovision Asia was much more affordable, he stated.

“Asia understands the brief — the kitschy costumes, the dance music,” he mentioned.

His top picks among the Asian performers were the Philippines’ Carmelle and Vietnam’s Toc Tien. “I think they hit the nail on the head with the song, staging, costume and traditional elements,” he mentioned.

Luca Cian, a professor of marketing at the University of Virginia who grew up in Italy, noted that Eurovision built a global fan base by offering a shared cultural experience.

“Millions of people across Europe watch it at the same moment,” he remarked. “Families have watch parties with food and drinks. There are public discussions. Rituals create community.”.

Carmen Chung, a British accountant, said she hijacked her family’s holiday in Bangkok to attend Eurovision Asia with her brother Garry Chung, a banker who lives in Hong Kong. “We were raised on Eurovision,” she said of their childhood in Yorkshire.

According to recent reports, european acts, she said, tend to copy whatever style of music won the previous year. “This year, because there are no expectations, everyone has just done their own thing,” she said. She and her brother said they were rooting for Bangladesh’s Beatmosphere, a beatboxing group that will perform an a cappella love song.

Industry observers note that martin Green, the director of the Eurovision Song Contest, noted that about half of the tickets for Saturday’s final were purchased by “super fans” from outside Asia. Organizers have kept the inaugural show modest, with 11 participating countries and a 5,000-seat venue.

Recent findings suggest that mr. Andrea said he didn’t mind the small scale.

Recent findings suggest that “I’m O.K. with humble beginnings as long as it keeps growing every year,” he said.

The Thai pop star Jeff Satur, a guest performer, got the high-camp memo.

The presenters are talking to the artists in the green room and trying to get them to talk excitedly about Bulgaria, the country that will host the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest. The winner tonight might get to perform at that event. That seems to be making this show less about Asia itself than a spin-off of the main Eurovision event.

Eurovision voting involves two parts. Juries representing music industry professionals from each country are allocated half the votes, and the viewing public decides the other half. To try to build tension, the show always announces the jury votes first by going live to representatives from each country who reveals their top acts. In the European edition of the contest, some of those spokespeople are celebrities, and often they try to give mini speeches or make jokes. This part of the show is always awful. You have been warned.

According to recent reports, there are a lot of European expatriates in this crowd. That much is obvious when Bulgaria’s Dara, the winner of this year’s Eurovision, takes the stage with her winning song, “Bangaranga.” Some fans even danced along with her choreography!

Mohamad Iqbal Dzulqarnain, an Aina Abdul fan in Kuala Lumpur, stated he felt her performance was better than the recording version.

Industry observers note that “She left no crumbs,” he said. “She is going to win the contest.”.

Alex Marshall and Francesca Regalado.

For a competition meant to introduce the diversity of Asian pop music to the world, the lineup for the first Eurovision Song Contest Asia on Saturday had several notable absences.

For starters, the continent’s four most populous nations — China, India, Pakistan and Indonesia — were not there. Even Japan, a country globally considered a cultural powerhouse, was absent.

That left some of the region’s best-known musical cultures out of the mix. India has Bollywood hits. China has produced both Mandopop and Cantopop, the genre associated with Hong Kong pop stars. JPop was once huge across Asia.

As a result, the only large pop powerhouse in this contest was South Korea.

China’s absence is relatively simple to explain. Performers are entered by local broadcasters, and Eurovision has long had a messy relationship with China’s, which are heavily regulated and try to reflect the government’s social and political values. Mango TV once had a deal to broadcast the high-camp Eurovision to Chinese viewers, but Eurovision abruptly canceled it in 2018 after Mango TV censored acts whose performances featured gay themes. It also blurred rainbow flags in the performance arena.

Frank-Dieter Freiling, a former Eurovision official, mentioned in an interview that such censorship was against Eurovision’s values and that the show’s organizers had historically barred broadcasters from airing the competition with delays.

Industry observers note that it’s less clear why broadcasters from India, Pakistan, Japan and Indonesia did not participate. Assaf Blecher, Eurovision Asia’s executive producer, mentioned that conversations with Chinese, Japanese and Indian broadcasters had not concluded in time. But he insisted that they “are knocking on our door.”.

Not participating saved those countries the potential embarrassment of being the regional power that comes in last.

In a recent development, just look to Europe, where Britain and Germany often perform badly at Eurovision. In this year’s show, Britain’s Look Mum No Computer placed last, scoring only one point, while Germany finished third from last. Whenever that happens, political commentators give interviews suggesting that the results reflect those countries’ poor standing across Europe.

Here at the watch party in Kathmandu, Pratik’s relatives are happy with his performance.

“His voice was cracking during the selection round in Nepal,” said Sunita Rai, his sister-in-law. “Today’s performance was much more powerful.”.

In a recent development, his relatives have been on social media all night, urging their friends who live overseas to vote for him. (You can’t vote for your own country’s performer.).

The presenters have just declared a technical concern! When Laos’s Thinla performed earlier, she had an earpiece problem and was unable to hear her own music. So that explains why she sang so out of tune. They’re now playing a recording of an earlier performance to everyone to try to ensure the event is fair.

Rizal Kamal, a senior adviser to the Arts, Live Festival and Events Association, an entertainment nonprofit based in Malaysia, said he felt that Aina Abdul was the right singer to represent the country at Eurovision.

“Aina is seasoned in major competitions and she knows how to wow both the judges and the audience,” he said. “I am filled with pride.”.

Aina Abdul’s inventive wardrobe and her powerful voice sets her apart from the Asian peers, mentioned Adriana Syuhaidah, a fan in Kuala Lumpur.

“She is the Lady Gaga of Malaysia,” she remarked.

#12885. Crows can make decisions twice as fast as humans, scientists discover

Crows can make decisions twice as fast as humans, scientists discover

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (693 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, crows can make visual decisions twice as quickly as humans and monkeys, according to new research from the University of Tübingen.
  • Sources indicate that the findings, published in the journal Science, offer new insight into how bird brains process information and make decisions.
  • Crows Make Rapid Decisions With Remarkable Accuracy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, crows can make visual decisions twice as quickly as humans and monkeys, according to new research from the University of Tübingen. In experiments involving two carrion crows, the birds needed an average of just 235 milliseconds to determine which way a pattern of moving dots was traveling and respond with their choice. Despite their remarkable speed, they remained highly accurate.

Sources indicate that the findings, published in the journal Science, offer new insight into how bird brains process information and make decisions. Researchers Philipp Schmidbauer and Professor Andreas Nieder from the University of Tübingen's Institute of Neurobiology found that the crows' rapid responses were accompanied by equally impressive activity in their brain cells.

Crows Make Rapid Decisions With Remarkable Accuracy.

It has been revealed that to test the birds' decision-making abilities, the researchers presented them with moving dots on a touchscreen. The crows had to determine whether most of the dots were traveling left or right, then indicate their answer by pecking a target on the corresponding side of the screen.

The birds performed remarkably well, even when the direction of movement was difficult to identify. "Even when the patterns of motion were hard to recognize, the crows' decisions were still better than random choices," Philipp Schmidbauer reports, "and with clear signals, they achieved an accuracy of nearly 100 percent.".

The results indicated that crows could evaluate visual information and make accurate choices in a fraction of a second. To understand how their brains accomplished this, the researchers examined the activity of individual neurons as the birds completed the task.

Crow Brains Begin Processing Decisions in Just 70 Milliseconds.

The team recorded neural activity in a part of the bird brain called the nidopallium caudolaterale. This region plays an key role in processing information and making decisions, much like the prefrontal cortex in the human brain.

Recent findings suggest that the recordings revealed that the crows' brains began distinguishing between the two possible directions almost immediately. Just 70 milliseconds after the moving dots appeared, neurons associated with the different choices were already showing distinct patterns of activity.

According to recent reports, these signals emerged well before the birds physically responded. As the crows evaluated the moving dots, neural activity steadily increased until it reached a threshold associated with making a decision. The activity reflected both how clearly the dots indicated a particular direction and which direction the bird ultimately selected.

Different Brain Structures, Similar Decision-Making Processes.

One of the most intriguing findings is that crows appear to make decisions using neural processes similar to those found in humans and other primates, even though their brains are organized very differently.

"These findings show that neuronal dynamics in the avian brain are consistent with established models of decision-making in humans and non-human primates," indicates Andreas Nieder.

In a recent development, unlike mammals, birds do not have a cerebral cortex organized into layers. Nevertheless, their brains appear capable of following the same fundamental principles for evaluating evidence and reaching decisions. In this visual task, the crows completed that process twice as promptly as primates.

Industry observers note that the researchers suggest that this exceptional speed could reflect the demands birds have faced throughout their evolution. Rapidly interpreting visual information and responding with precise movements are especially important for animals that fly and use their beaks to interact with their surroundings.

"Birds rely on their vision to carry out precise, rapid maneuvers during flight and to guide their beaks towards objects when foraging," Nieder explains.

In a recent development, however, the exact biological mechanisms responsible for the crows' speed advantage remain unknown. Further studies will be needed to determine how their differently structured brains can make comparable visual decisions so much faster than those of humans and monkeys.

Tech Report: Skydance outlines its $6 billion in planned cost savings. Here's the breakdown

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Skydance is pulling back the curtain on how it looks to achieve at least $6 billion in cost savings in the next three years.
  • "By combining two global streaming services, two film and TV studio groups, two television portfolios, and overlapping corporate functions, we can reduce duplicative spend across an expense base of more than $50 billion," the organization wrote in a letter to shareholders Monday as part of Paramount Skydance's third-quarter earnings release.
  • Skydance, the company formed by the combination of Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Skydance is pulling back the curtain on how it looks to achieve at least $6 billion in cost savings in the next three years.

"By combining two global streaming services, two film and TV studio groups, two television portfolios, and overlapping corporate functions, we can reduce duplicative spend across an expense base of more than $50 billion," the organization wrote in a letter to shareholders Monday as part of Paramount Skydance's third-quarter earnings release.

Skydance, the company formed by the combination of Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery, mentioned it projects at least $2.2 billion in cost reductions from eliminating "redundant back-office and corporate functions," including eliminating management layers and ramping the use of artificial intelligence. Those savings also account for "rationalizing" its office footprint.

Recent findings suggest that skydance expects at least $1 billion in savings from streamlining marketing and promotional spending. And around $1.4 billion in savings will come from unifying its streaming businesses and broadcast architecture and integrating back-end technology.

A final $1.4 billion in savings will be tied to "optimizing third-party spend," eliminating overlapping expenses, and consolidating purchasing decisions to one centralized group, Skydance stated.

"We are confident in achieving these savings, drawing on our playbook from Paramount," the firm wrote. "That program is on track to achieve over $2.7 billion in run-rate efficiencies by the end of 2026.".

Some of that cost-cutting has already begun.

Last month, Skydance began offering voluntary buyouts to employees ahead of official layoffs. At the same time, the manufacturer adopted a five-day-per-week in-office policy. Additionally, last week saw the departure of eight executives — four from Warner Bros. and four from Paramount.

The company has previously stated it looks to eventually merge the Paramount+ and HBO Max streaming services into a single platform.

On Monday, Skydance said it would take the first step toward that goal early next year, offering a bundle of the streaming services "at an even greater value.".

Recent findings suggest that co-CEO Ynon Kreiz told investors during the company's earnings call that Skydance is also looking for ways to optimize its content budget. The company spends more than $30 billion annually on shows and films.

"As one manufacturer, we can make smarter choices about how we distribute and monetize both new content and library content," Kreiz mentioned.

In a recent development, skydance noted that it's expecting a $200 million headwind in the fourth quarter from theatrical underperformances at Warner Bros. studio related to already released titles and upcoming releases.

The company will also utilize AI to speed up production and decrease costs to make films, co-CEO and chairman David Ellison noted on the call.

"We think these tools will help unlock more original storytelling by being able to make the budget more digestible to be able to take that amount of risk," Ellison mentioned.

The updates came alongside third-quarter results for the legacy Paramount Skydance organization that included revenue of $7.03 billion, which was roughly in line with StreetAccount estimates of $7.04 billion, and adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization of $1 billion, topping StreetAccount estimates of $913.5 million.

However, adjusted earnings per share of 45 cents were not immediately comparable to StreetAccount EPS estimates.

The results don't include the impact of the Warner Bros. Discovery acquisition, which closed after the end of the third quarter.

Skydance detailed business units of the combined entity, including studios, direct-to-consumer and TV, and remarked it will provide full-year guidance during its fourth-quarter earnings report early next year.

Recent findings suggest that nessa Carey's career has straddled both academia and industry. “In industry you tend to have much more of a sense of shared purpose, and you operate in teams,” she notes.

It has been revealed that academia, on the other hand, is more personality-driven, and feels more individualistic. “Failure tends to be very binary: you either failed or you succeeded, and it's very personal,” she adds.

But as global research collaborations become more multidisciplinary, a culture change is needed in higher education, says Carey, who now runs a training business that supports biotechnology and drug discovery spinoffs.

Earlier this year, Carey spoke at a one-day conference on failure in science, with a focus on careers and innovation. It was held at Imperial College London in partnership with Nature.

In the penultimate episode of a six-part podcast series that revisits some of the conference themes, Carey urges academia to look at how industry handles failure, where struggling projects are abandoned more promptly.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03772-y.

Is innovation as slow as it's often labelled?

Oftentimes we talk about innovation being slow, but in fact, you know, many of us feel like we're living in an ever-changing society.

After the failure and innovation session, the chair, Dr Nejra van Zalk, a design psychologist at Imperial College London, reported back to delegates attending the Failure in Science Conference, held in April this year.

[Recording from the Failure In Science conference].

It has been revealed that why do we choose innovation in one area of healthcare, for example, and not in another area? And who makes those decisions?

Why do we focus on obesity drugs and pump money into that, rather than helping to fix musculoskeletal complications in children who would have much better outcomes over a lifetime.

I'm Dr Stephen Webster, director of The Good Science Project at Imperial College London, a programme that examines what we like about research culture, and what we don't.

And in episode five of this series, we explore the business of discovery.

To put it bluntly, when it comes to failure, could universities learn a thing or two from industry?

[Recording from the Failure In Science conference].

How can we safely incorporate failure into our working models?

Can we look to industry to see how they're doing it when they actually, they cut their losses sooner and they abandon projects quicker and they can quantify their risks in different ways than we can in academia.

Could we learn lessons from that?

In a recent development, so my name is Nessa Carey, I'm a PhD scientist. And I've worked in academia, in industry, and as a freelancer. So I've kind of done a lot of things over the space of my career.

Sources indicate that oh, so so many failures. I started out with the classic academic failures of having grants rejected, having papers rejected.

According to recent reports, in industry, you get things like programmes that you simply can't keep running. And also if you move to industry, you will be made redundant at some point or another.

And it's very easy, particularly the first time, to view that as a personal failure, but as you get more experienced, you realize it's just about organizations, it's just about shifting priorities, and actually it's not that significant a deal.

Sources indicate that so your definition of failure changes as your career changes. And also as you get older, I think it changes as well.

[Recording from the Failure In Science Conference].

I wanted to ask us, and perhaps ask the panel: as society, and this is not simply a UK perspective I don't think, have we become hyper risk averse?

Is that the direction that we're heading in?

And if so, where is the space for failure, and particularly the space for failure in science?

So, in the opening session of the conference at Imperial College, Professor Jem Woods suggested that we have become too risk averse and that that has really negative consequences, for example in academia.

And I think I absolutely agree with that, but I don't think it's just academia that is negatively impacted by this.

And I think the conversation has shifted, and not necessarily in a way that's helpful. And I think it's particularly a lot of pressure on younger people.

In a recent development, so I do quite a lot of outreach work in schools, and I see young students who are under enormous pressure to do well at their GCSEs or their A levels or whatever is the equivalent in another country, because they have to get onto the right course at the right college. They have to get a career trajectory that's working in the right direction.

And so I think there's a much bigger fear of failure because the stakes have been made artificially high.

In reality, as long as you do a course that you're happy on at a university where you're happy living, you'll do fine.

But we've built in this terrible sequential success demand on the young, and I think it's also exacerbated by [the fact we] we now have much more public discourse because we have social media, and everybody posts their triumphs. Everybody posts their success. You look at LinkedIn, and it's just full of people celebrating their promotion, their latest certificate, etc.

The trouble is that's not real. That's not how life generally progresses. You try stuff, you stuff up, you learn from it, and you move on.

And if we always class that as failure rather than a normal part of learning, then I think we do create really, really big problems for the future because everybody will try and stay inside their comfort zone.

Everybody will be frightened of doing something wrong.

It's a massive problem in science because science thrives on innovation, but it's a big problem in any creative sector, and we run the risk of situations where people would rather do nothing than take a risk.

And you see that in organizations as well, and that's a really big problem.

I think what academia could do with learning from industry in terms of failure is to depersonalize it somewhat.

I think that's extremely difficult to do in reality.

One of the things that I enjoyed about working in industry, as opposed to working in academia, is in industry you tend to have much more of a sense of shared purpose, and you operate in teams. And yes, you may be the leader of a team, but you're still a team.

Academia, I find generally is much more individualistic.

If you have a much more individualistic environment, it is much harder to acknowledge failure as being simply a consequence of good decisions that are made by a team.

In a recent development, in academia, failure tends to be very binary: you either failed or you succeeded, and it's very personal. And it's very personal, in particular, to the Principal Investigators.

That's very different from industry.

In industry, you can be doing really interesting work on a project, and then you do the killer experiment and realize your project can't go anywhere. And as a team, and as the leader of a team, you make the decision that that project needs to be terminated.

Now, that in academia would feel like failure because you can't then go on and apply for grants for it.

In industry, there's much more an emphasis in good companies on “did we make the right decision?”, and if you made the right decision, then the target failed or the program failed, but you didn't necessarily fail as an individual.

And I think it's that difference between viewing things as projects and teams and viewing things as individual endeavours.

And given that more and more science is becoming multidisciplinary, multi-team, it would make so much more sense if academia could start to change its culture towards that, because on the whole, the big papers that we see coming out now – they're big team efforts, and yet reward still tends to remain very individual.

It has been revealed that so it's a structural concern. It's not just about people.

I think academia could adapt well by adopting some of the good managerial and people development skills of industry.

Academia is, in my experience, much more driven by personalities, and that creates enormous emotional heft behind things.

It has been revealed that in industry, of course, there are major personalities. There are in every sector, but because you're working as an organization, you don't have quite this same strange mix of your personal emotional life with your professional life, and so you can fail professionally without it having quite the same impact on you as an individual emotionally, if that makes sense.

Something that the industry has got very, very good on is identifying killer experiments, carrying them out, and doing the thing that is considered a cliche now – but is absolutely critical – of fail fast, fail promptly, fail early, fail cheaply: that you don't keep trying to progress something that cannot get to the end point that you need.

And I think industry, on the whole, is very good at that. It used to be very bad. It's got better.

Sources indicate that academia is terrible at that in my experience, in that what will happen is somebody has their favourite target, their favourite process, their favourite enzyme, and they just keep working on it because they have a reputation for that and because they can keep working on it, rather than thinking “do you know what? It'd be really good to set up this experiment, see if I'm on the right track, and if I'm not, I'll kill it.” Instead, what they tend to do is just find other things they can keep working on in the same field.

Now, sometimes that's entirely appropriate, and sometimes it's that real curiosity-led stuff that takes us in a weird direction and opens up all sorts of things.

But there is always a risk that you will just keep chugging away at something because you know you'll at least get a couple of papers out of it, or because your PhD student needs the data for their thesis, etc.

It's a very different environment, and so it's not that I'm saying we should import everything from industry into academia, but I do think sometimes academia could benefit from the critical thinking of industry that goes: take away the emotion and actually look at this from scratch and say, “would we carry on if we were starting now?”.

[Recording from the Failure In Science Conference].

Sources indicate that so I mentioned these grand challenges; We often talk about them in science circles, The grand challenges. What's the role of science in helping society address these grand challenges?

And the emergence of innovation in technologies, I think has now switched to hyper disruptive technologies, and that's specifically around how we manage, or [how] information is managed. (When I say we, maybe it's not managed).

And then societal and community and individual access to those innovations in technology, and I think it's often labelled as ‘The BBC's Post-Truth Society’, because there were many of the BBC journalists (and some of them may be in the audience I don't know) who talked a lot about this emergence of that technological system in the post-truth society. And we have real questions in science to answer around that understanding of the way that information is generated and the way it's perceived and used societally.

So, in the opening session, Jem Woods was talking about the fact that there's been a drop of trust in science, and I wouldn't say it's just science.

There's a drop in trust in multiple areas, including in our trust in politicians, and our trust in writers, and our trust in the media.

And I think it's phenomenally vital that scientists continue to do their work to the highest level of probity, and the vast majority of scientists do that, and that is true whatever sector you're in.

Scientists are remarkably similar, whether they're in academia or they're in industry; they're there because they want to do good science.

Recent findings suggest that I think it's vital that everybody continues to do really good science. I think it's also vital, though, that we do challenge one another appropriately and professionally.

But what is also really key is that scientists continue to communicate, to a wider public, what is important about science and the scientific method, and also to be very upfront about the limitations of our research and the limitations of our findings.

This again, I think, ties into the issue of success and failure, because one of the things that's happened is public engagement and communication of science have been added to the academic workload.

The academic workload never decreases; fresh stuff always gets added to it, and it becomes another box to tick.

And there is a risk that people not only need to do good science, but they need to do science that can be communicated well.

And I think the most dangerous thing for academia is that it's constantly under pressure to justify why its science is being done. What is the benefit, the direct, very tangible benefit for humanity?

And that creates pressure to overstate one's outcomes, to be too black and white about it because black and white stories sell – it's much easier to sell a black and white story – but we have to be really careful not to do that because every time we do that and get challenged, we undermine the faith not so much in our science, because each member of the public has probably forgotten us, but the faith in science itself.

We shouldn't be scared of saying it's complicated, and so I think there is a real risk there that by being unsubtle about how we communicate our science, we actually undermine faith in a field which has essentially added enormous benefit to humanity and to the planet, and we need to be very careful not to lose that.

So I've worked in the field of innovation for about 25 years, and it's just as difficult now as it was 25 years ago.

Recent findings suggest that but I think there are particular concerns now that we're facing as a world that we didn't face back then. AI is the obvious one of having created a technology that actually may outrun us, and no one's quite clear how that's going to play out now.

But I think there are bigger issues at stake here as well.

I think it's very difficult when so much science is being published and being done to work out which of it genuinely has the potential to shift the needle on a particular issue.

It has been revealed that but I think it's actually at risk of us having such a focus on innovation, in the sense of ‘where's the next great widget? Where's the next great drug?’, that we forget that technological innovation may not actually be what we require to solve particular problems.

So one of the things that really really frustrates me is seeing more and more emphasis, and more and more funding, in climate change going into carbon capture.

Carbon capture at scale is an entirely unproven technology, and it's not clear at all that it can solve the climate change problem.

We do, however, know that moving to electric cars makes a huge difference, and yet we are not in the UK legislating to do that appropriately.

We also have a situation where drug companies are spending billions of dollars to develop drugs for chronic health conditions that we actually know are caused essentially by social inequality and poverty.

We would be so much better as societies if we would put our money into more equitable healthcare systems, more equitable food availability systems.

We would have an enormous return on investment, but we don't see that return on investment for a very long time, and it's not a capitalist return on investment, it's a government return on investment.

So my concern is that our biggest failures will come because we constantly try to ‘tech’ our way out of problems that don't actually require technological solutions.

They require different, longer-term, less glossy solutions that don't make money for companies, and our systems on the whole run in a way that have placed an awful lot of, say, healthcare and environmental responsibilities and opportunities on significant capitalist companies, when actually they are not the right structure to deliver those outcomes.

According to recent reports, so that is where I think our biggest failures will come: We will ‘tech’ when we shouldn't be ‘tech-ing’. We will try and ‘tech’ very expensively when actually we could have made smaller investments with much more impact.

And it is deeply frustrating to me that also we as scientists will go “don't worry, we'll come up with a technological solution.” instead of saying “we may never come up with a technological solution, but if you talk to our friends in the social sciences, they already know what needs to be done. Why on earth aren't you doing this?” And that, I think, is a failure on the part of science to pretend that we are the ones who will solve everything.

  • Recent findings suggest that researchers at Istanbul Technical University (ITU) have explored that possibility by taking a fresh look at an established alternative theory of gravity.
  • Industry observers note that the research was conducted within Akarsu's group at ITU, alongside postdoctoral researcher Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that for decades, scientists have generally assumed that dark energy, the mysterious component thought to be responsible for the Universe's accelerating expansion, has remained constant throughout cosmic history. That long-standing assumption is now facing fresh scrutiny. Observations from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), which is constructing the largest three-dimensional map of the Universe, suggest that dark energy's influence may have changed over billions of years. Although the evidence is not yet strong enough to establish a discovery, it has renewed interest in a fundamental question: Could dark energy evolve rather than remain constant?

Recent findings suggest that researchers at Istanbul Technical University (ITU) have explored that possibility by taking a fresh look at an established alternative theory of gravity. In a 2025 study published in Physical Review D, an international team led by Prof. Özgür Akarsu of ITU's Department of Physics investigated a mathematical possibility that previous researchers had largely overlooked. Their analysis revealed a surprising scenario in which the effective density of dark energy was negative during the Universe's early history before eventually becoming positive.

Industry observers note that the research was conducted within Akarsu's group at ITU, alongside postdoctoral researcher Dr. N. Merve Uzun and doctoral student Bilal Bulduk. The team also collaborated with Prof. Nihan Katırcı of Doğuş University, who previously worked as a postdoctoral researcher in Akarsu's group, and Prof. Antonio De Felice of Kyoto University's Yukawa Institute for Theoretical Physics, an internationally recognized center for theoretical physics.

An Overlooked Possibility in Einstein's Theory of Gravity.

The discovery came from examining a part of an existing theory that had received relatively little attention. Rather than proposing an entirely upcoming explanation for dark energy, the researchers revisited a framework known as teleparallel f(T) gravity.

Einstein's general theory of relativity explains gravity through the curvature of spacetime. Teleparallel gravity takes a different mathematical approach, describing gravity through a property called torsion. Scientists have spent years studying modified versions of this framework to investigate whether gravity itself might account for the Universe's accelerating expansion.

Earlier investigations of an exponential form of teleparallel gravity had concentrated on one particular set of mathematical solutions. This approach reflected a familiar assumption inherited from general relativity: dark energy should always have a positive density.

Recent findings suggest that akarsu and his colleagues decided to investigate what would happen if that restriction were removed. By considering a previously neglected branch of the theory, they uncovered a substantially different picture of how the Universe might have evolved.

Dark Energy May Have Switched From Negative to Positive.

The team's calculations showed that two distinct cosmic histories could emerge even when the Universe contains the same amount of matter today.

One mathematical solution closely resembles the standard model of cosmology. The other predicts that effective dark energy had a negative density in the distant past. According to this second possibility, the density reached zero at approximately redshift 1.5, corresponding to roughly 9.5 billion years ago, before becoming positive and remaining that way.

Sources indicate that what makes the result particularly interesting is that the researchers did not need to introduce an additional adjustable parameter to produce this behavior. Instead, the determining factor is related to the Universe's present matter density, which selects the mathematical branch. As a result, the model retains the same six cosmological parameters used in the standard ΛCDM model.

Industry observers note that the theory also avoids an important potential problem. Although it predicts behavior that differs from Einstein's gravity across enormous cosmic distances, its departures from general relativity become naturally suppressed in dense environments. This allows the alternative solution to remain compatible with the highly accurate measurements of gravity made throughout the Solar System.

A Possible Explanation for the Hubble Tension.

The latest findings build on years of research into whether dark energy could have changed sign during the Universe's history.

Akarsu and his collaborators previously developed a framework called the sign-switching ΛCDM (ΛsCDM) model. In this scenario, the cosmological constant changes from negative to positive several billion years after the Big Bang.

In a recent development, previous analyses found that a change in the sign of dark energy's density could agree with DESI observations while potentially reducing several unresolved disagreements in cosmology. One of the most significant is the Hubble tension, the persistent discrepancy between different methods of measuring the Universe's present expansion rate.

According to recent reports, however, an important question remained unanswered. What underlying physical process could cause dark energy to undergo such a reversal?

Sources indicate that the latest research offers a possible mechanism. Instead of requiring scientists to prescribe a sign change as part of the model, the reversal arises naturally from the mathematical structure of the modified gravity theory.

Akarsu explained why investigating an overlooked solution proved so valuable.

"For several years we have been studying a scenario in which dark energy switches sign, and it has held up remarkably well against data such as DESI's. The open question was what physical mechanism could produce such behavior. So we deliberately looked at a branch of a well-known theory of gravity that had been set aside because it violates the usual expectation that the dark energy density stays positive. The sign change emerged naturally from the theory itself.".

DESI Observations Raise Latest Questions About Dark Energy.

The theoretical findings have become especially relevant as astronomers gather increasingly detailed measurements of cosmic expansion.

Industry observers note that DESI tracks the locations of millions of galaxies and quasars, allowing researchers to reconstruct how the Universe has expanded across billions of years. In March 2025, the DESI collaboration released findings based on its first three years of observations.

When combined with measurements of the cosmic microwave background, supernovae, and weak gravitational lensing, the results strengthened earlier indications that dark energy might not behave like a fixed cosmological constant.

These findings do not yet establish that dark energy changes over time. The statistical significance depends on which observational datasets are combined, and the evidence remains below the threshold required to claim a definitive discovery. Nevertheless, the possibility has motivated scientists to investigate alternative descriptions of cosmic expansion.

Recent findings suggest that DESI has now completed its planned five-year survey, observing more than 47 million galaxies and quasars. The complete dataset will provide an even more demanding test of whether the apparent changes in dark energy persist as measurements become more precise.

Recent findings suggest that the timing is also noteworthy. The ITU-led team's research was initially submitted in October 2024, several months before DESI revealed its March 2025 findings. The researchers have not yet tested their model against the complete DESI dataset, making that comparison an important next step.

Could the Universe's Accelerating Expansion Be Slowing?

The significance of the proposed model extends beyond its prediction that dark energy's density may have changed sign.

Because the alternative solution emerges from a specific theory of gravity, it makes predictions about both cosmic expansion and how gravity behaves across the Universe. These predictions give astronomers ways to investigate whether the proposed cosmic history is consistent with observations.

Recent findings suggest that measurements of how galaxies and larger structures form and grow will be particularly important. Researchers can also examine how gravity bends light and how the Universe's expansion has changed over time. Among the most useful observational tests are structure growth, redshift-space distortions, and weak gravitational lensing.

Although comprehensive testing remains necessary, the initial results offer reasons for further investigation.

In an extended version of the theory that includes a cosmological constant, the researchers found that the model could remain consistent with observations of the cosmic microwave background while allowing the higher present-day expansion rates obtained from local measurements. This makes it a potentially useful approach to understanding the Hubble tension.

Recent findings suggest that the extended model also permits another intriguing possibility: the acceleration of the Universe's expansion could have weakened or even stopped in the relatively recent cosmic past. Recent studies examining DESI observations have raised similar questions about whether cosmic acceleration has remained steady.

Recent findings suggest that importantly, neither the proposed dark energy reversal nor a recent slowdown in cosmic acceleration has been established as an observational fact. Both remain possibilities that must be tested against increasingly precise data.

Revisiting Gravity Could Reveal a Different Cosmic History.

The research highlights how familiar scientific theories can contain possibilities that were missed because earlier investigations relied on restrictive assumptions.

In this case, allowing effective dark energy to have a negative density exposed an alternative evolutionary history within an already established mathematical framework. The researchers suggest that examining similarly overlooked solutions in other modified gravity theories could lead to additional insights.

Ultimately, the strength of the new explanation will depend on how well it reproduces the Universe astronomers actually observe. The full DESI dataset and other cosmological measurements will help determine whether this unusual version of cosmic history deserves a place alongside established explanations.

"We identified an alternative path for the Universe within an existing theory. The next step is to test it rigorously against the full observational data. The preliminary picture is encouraging, and we are particularly interested in what it may tell us about the Hubble tension," said Prof. Özgür Akarsu.

Nvidia Was Already in Trouble Before the Jensen Huang Mess

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1215 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nvidia played a key role enabling the AI gold rush thanks in large part to its recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang.
  • According to recent reports, but just as he’s leaving, the company has a growing list of competitors with a range of new, advanced technology breathing down its neck.
  • Recent findings suggest that “Everything sold today was designed two to three years ago,” says the CEO of a large AI firm, who spoke to WIRED on condition of anonymity to avoid hurting business relationships.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia played a key role enabling the AI gold rush thanks in large part to its recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang. Huang was a master of foreseeing technological changes, investing in chips to train AI earlier than most.

According to recent reports, but just as he’s leaving, the company has a growing list of competitors with a range of new, advanced technology breathing down its neck. For Nvidia, where CFO Colette Kress has now taken the reins, the timing isn’t great.

Recent findings suggest that “Everything sold today was designed two to three years ago,” says the CEO of a large AI firm, who spoke to WIRED on condition of anonymity to avoid hurting business relationships. Kress, or whoever replaces her permanently, will have to chart the course that the chip industry will take two years from now, the CEO says.

Already, competitors have started to move in.

Industry observers note that nvidia dominates the market for AI accelerators, capturing 80 percent of sales, according to Silicon Analysis. Longtime nemesis AMD is now making a concerted effort to build competitive AI chips. Its share of the market has crept up from just two percent in 2022 to between 7 and 10 percent in 2026.

Substantial US cloud players—Google, Amazon, and Microsoft—are all developing more specialized chips to power the training and serving of AI models. Each has seen similar gains. These companies are designing their own silicon to reduce costs and to gain some independence from Nvidia.

Industry observers note that several startups now offer more specialized chips that promise improvements over Nvidia’s core products. Cerebras, for instance, sells giant ones meant to power giant AI models. AMD recently bought Taalas, a company that burns models’ weights into silicon to make computations ultra efficient. Using these chips requires rewriting a lot of code, however, to make them work with cutting-edge AI models.

Recent findings suggest that patrick Moorhead, chief analyst at MoorInStrat, a company that tracks the chip industry, states the rise of AI agents makes inference, or running models that have already been trained, more crucial. That’s an area where Nvidia has less of an edge compared to cloud hyperscalers and startups. Nvidia did, however, acquire a startup making specialized chips, called Groq, in December of 2025.

And because of the rise in AI assistants and agents, there’s also growing demand for general purpose central processing units (CPUs), Moorhead said, an area where Nvidia barely competes.

Sources indicate that nvidia still maintains a huge lead in AI thanks to Huang’s foresight. Huang cofounded the company in 1993 to design graphics chips for PCs. In the mid-2010s, he saw the promise of AI. He funded academic research on the topic, developed software to support AI engineering, and gave hardware to labs and startups.

In 2022, ChatGPT took AI mainstream and sales of Nvidia chips skyrocketed. The company’s revenue went from $26.91 billion in January 2022 to $215.94 billion in January 2026. The challenges it faces may not be existential—but they do add up, especially on a global scale.

In a recent development, while Nvidia’s fortunes have risen in the US, they have declined in the world’s other substantial market for AI: China. Washington is trying to restrict access to its most advanced chips, while Beijing is trying to develop its own chip industry. Nvidia is not allowed to sell its most powerful chips in China, but it can sell previous generations. Sales of these chips as well as non AI chips doubled over the past year, but China now accounts for only eight percent of the company’s overall revenue, compared with 20 percent in 2024, according to its fillings. It remains unclear how many chips exported to other countries may either end up in China or end up being used remotely by Chinese firms.

Huawei, a Chinese tech giant targeted with US sanctions for several years, has developed upcoming kinds of supercomputers that harness many more chips than usual to train and run AI models. Some Chinese AI companies, such as Z.ai, which makes one of the world’s best open source models, say they’ve trained their models entirely using Huawei’s chips. If Chinese open-weight models gain traction in other countries, it could create a market for Chinese chips elsewhere.

According to recent reports, huang’s dealings with China played a major role in his downfall. He had a romantic relationship with Huang Le, also known as Alice Huang, a Chinese executive at a Singaporean firm called Megaspeed who the US government suspects of being an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. Megaspeed and its subsidiaries have reportedly imported between $4.6 and $7.5 billion Nvidia chips into southeast Asia. Reports suggest that the company may have provided access to the chips to Chinese AI firms.

Babak Minovi, a senior analyst at the Eurasia Group, a consultancy that focuses on technology and geopolitics, indicates Huang was right to point out that cutting off access to China would empower domestic rivals. “Huang was taking a pragmatic line, and he knows competition,” he says.

Sources indicate that even in markets that it dominates, Nvidia may turn out to be a victim of its own success. The AI models built using Nvidia’s chip are automating the very elements of coding, data analysis, and scientific research that help design chips.

Recent findings suggest that most chip design firms use specialized AI models to arrange components on processors—something that traditionally required deep engineering expertise and experience. And both OpenAI and Anthropic have recently touted the ability of their newest models to design electronics from scratch.

Sources indicate that moorhead says the shift towards AI chip design may not pose a huge threat to Nvidia because it’s riding the same wave. “They have access to AI too,” he notes.

In a recent development, but Moorhead says the way AI models can now promptly rewrite code to run on different hardware may prove a problem. For years, Nvidia has attracted developers by providing software that makes it easy to write programs and build models for its silicon. Its Compute Unified Device Architecture, or CUDA, has long been seen as a moat to ensure AI companies continue to rely on Nvidia chips.

But AI models are now so good at reading and writing code that they can port an AI model over to a competitor's silicon at speed.

Wafer, a startup that uses AI to port models to AMD and then serves them more cheaply, has seen revenue grow spectacularly in recent months, boasts CEO Emilio Andere.

Sources indicate that every time a major new open weight model is released Wafer can have it running on AMD hardware at least 80 percent as efficiently within hours, he says. Andere says AI is getting so capable that his engineers barely have to edit or review the code.

Dan Hutchinson, a veteran chip analyst, says Nvidia may be entering its “Intel swan moment,” referring to the 2019 replacement of engineering-focused CEO Brian Krzanich with its CFO Bob Swan. (Sound familiar? Krzanich also resigned after a relationship with an employee; Huang is alleged to have had multiple.) From there, the company’s focus shifted to sales more than technical progress. Bureaucracy ballooned and revenue tanked.

“Nvidia is now an Intel waiting to happen,” he says.

Industry News: Why hasn't the 'Blaze Star' exploded yet? Astronomers weigh in on what to expect

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (967 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that for the past two years, stargazers have waited with bated breath for a "latest" light to appear in the night sky, born of one of the most cataclysmic events known to occur in the cosmos — a nova explosion.
  • Coronae Borealis — or T CrB for short — isn't a single star, but rather a binary system containing a dense white dwarf star and a bloated red giant.
  • "T CrB *will* erupt sometime soon," Bradley Schaefer of the Louisiana State University Department of Physics and Astronomy told Space.com in an email.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that for the past two years, stargazers have waited with bated breath for a "latest" light to appear in the night sky, born of one of the most cataclysmic events known to occur in the cosmos — a nova explosion. But what is the "Blaze Star" T. Coronae Borealis, and why is it so difficult to predict when its overdue brightening will occur? We turned to the experts to find out.

Sources indicate that T. Coronae Borealis — or T CrB for short — isn't a single star, but rather a binary system containing a dense white dwarf star and a bloated red giant. Over a period of around 80 years, the white dwarf's gravity strips material from the red giant until it hits a critical threshold. Next comes a dramatic nova explosion that causes the star to flare to 1,000 times its usual brightness before gradually settling down and repeating the cycle.

"T CrB *will* erupt sometime soon," Bradley Schaefer of the Louisiana State University Department of Physics and Astronomy told Space.com in an email. "Everyone is very confident on this. But we cannot make high-accuracy measures of the rate of gas falling onto the surface of the white dwarf, and we do not have a high accuracy measure of the trigger mass for the significant hydrogen bomb." Schaefer continued.

Historical observations reveal that the last nova eruption reached Earth in 1946, which places us well inside the window for another dramatic brightening of T. CrBb. However, the unpredictability of the white dwarf's feeding makes it difficult to pin down exactly when the explosion will become visible from Earth.

"The exact date of the upcoming T CrB eruption depends primarily on how fast the gas coming from its companion star is accumulating on the surface of the white dwarf," explained Schaefer. "When some specific trigger mass has accumulated, then T CrB will erupt. For the last 80 years, we have been watching the gas pile up on the white dwarf surface, and we know that it must be near the trigger threshold.".

Astronomers have tried to predict T CrB's brightening by comparing a recent fluctuation in the light of the distant star system to a similar event that occurred in the runup to the 1946 event.

Industry observers note that "There have already been some dimming and brightening episodes that caused excitement but did not yet turn into the main event," Elizabeth Hays, lab chief at NASA's Astroparticle Physics Laboratory at the Goddard Spaceflight Center, told Space.com in an email. "It is likely that the nova will happen in the next few years but we still don't know exactly when. I can't give you a guaranteed prediction, but I will be a little surprised if it gets to 2030, or 84 years past the last eruption.".

Industry observers note that hays notes that the intense light from the red giant dramatically outshines the dimmer white dwarf, making detailed observation challenging. There is also no way to precisely measure the temperature and pressure of the matter lurking near the surface of the smaller star. "Predicting nova explosions are a little like predicting the weather; conditions may be right but the timing of the storm can be uncertain.".

There'll be no visual warning of the eruption before it reaches Earth, though according to Hays there could be an early flash of light in the X-ray spectrum.

"The world's amateur astronomers have been doing an awesome job of keeping T CrB under hair-trigger monitoring roughly every minute or two, so when T CrB has brightened by around one magnitude, then alerts will spread around the world within minutes," said Schaefer.

Recent findings suggest that once the call goes out, telescopes and observatories around the world will kick into gear, running pre-prepared observation programmes to capitalize on the rare and cataclysmic event. "When the nuclear runaway process starts, it will take off and peak very promptly, in less than a day.".

The nova will see the star jump from its normal brightness of magnitude +10 — which is beyond the detection limit of the naked eye — to magnitude +1.7, making it appear as if a star brighter than the North Star Polaris has suddenly burst to life in the night sky.

It has been revealed that "The brightness will fall below naked-eye visibility in dark places within a couple of days and become too faint for binoculars within about a week," stated Hays. "Outside the visible band, for example, in radio, X-ray and gamma rays, light caused by the eruption will be visible for months or even years. ".

T CrB can be found glowing close to the magnitude +4.28 star Epsilon Coronae Borealis in the constellation Corona Borealis during the early evening in November, with the constellations of Hercules and Bootes on either side.

Sources indicate that it will dip below the horizon for viewers in the U.S. just a few hours after sunset, before re-emerging into the northeastern sky in the predawn hours.

Industry observers note that want to capture a photo of T. CrB when it erupts? Then be sure to read our guide to photographing the night sky, along with our picks of the best cameras, lenses and smart telescopes that are perfect for capturing the majesty of the starry realm.

Recent findings suggest that anthony Wood joined Space.com in April 2025 after contributing articles to outlets including IGN, Fresh Atlas and Gizmodo. He has a passion for the night sky, science, Hideo Kojima, and human space exploration, and can’t wait for the day when astronauts once again set foot on the moon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Geopolitics have long intruded on the Eurovision Song Contest. But they were not really a factor as the event prepared to expand into Asia for the first time.

That was still true as of Saturday evening, when the inaugural Eurovision Song Contest Asia took place in Bangkok.

Recent findings suggest that over the decades, Eurovision organizers have insisted that the contest is nonpolitical. Its organizers impose rules governing lyrics, political symbols and what can be broadcast. Even so, wars and diplomatic disputes have shaped who gets to sing, who stays home and what broadcasters are willing to air.

“Politics is why we watch Eurovision,” remarked Dean Vuletic, a historian of the show at the University of Luxembourg.

Here are some examples of geopolitics bleeding into the European edition of the contest:.

In 2009, less than a year after fighting a war with Russia, the former Soviet republic of Georgia planned to send a disco song called “We Don’t Wanna Put In” to Eurovision. Eurovision’s organizers remarked that the apparent dig at Vladimir Putin, then Russia’s prime minister, had to go. Georgia pulled out instead of changing it.

Industry observers note that in 2017, Russia pulled out of the contest in Kyiv after Ukraine barred its singer from entering the country. And five years later, after Russia introduced its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Eurovision barred Russia altogether.

It has been revealed that in 2024, the war in Gaza triggered mass protests over Israel’s participation. A bitter dispute over government influence on voting followed in 2025, and there were boycotts of the contest by five countries in 2026, the biggest crisis in Eurovision’s 70-year history.

The 11 Asian countries that sent artists to Saturday’s show have plenty of offstage geopolitical friction.

Cambodia, for example, is set to sing in Thailand’s capital less than a year after a border war between the two neighbors killed dozens and displaced hundreds of thousands. As fighting picked up last year, Cambodia withdrew its athletes from the Southeast Asian Games in Thailand, citing safety concerns.

#12874. Latest Update: The Sun unleashed a monster storm. Earth may have made it worse

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1298 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: The Sun unleashed a monster storm. Earth may have made it worse

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1298 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In May 2024, an extraordinary solar storm sent brilliant auroras across skies in parts of the world where the northern and southern lights are rarely visible.
  • Sources indicate that the event began when a large sunspot unleashed several powerful solar eruptions in rapid succession.
  • Industry observers note that for decades, researchers have debated where the particles that make up this ring current come from.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In May 2024, an extraordinary solar storm sent brilliant auroras across skies in parts of the world where the northern and southern lights are rarely visible. But the spectacular displays were only the most obvious signs of an enormous disturbance unfolding in space around Earth. Deep within the planet's magnetosphere, the vast region controlled by its magnetic field, scientists were witnessing something they had never directly measured before.

Sources indicate that the event began when a large sunspot unleashed several powerful solar eruptions in rapid succession. As enormous clouds of magnetized plasma raced through space, they combined before slamming into Earth's magnetosphere. The resulting storm produced the strongest magnetic disturbance ever measured in Earth's ring current, a vast region of electrically charged particles surrounding the planet.

Industry observers note that for decades, researchers have debated where the particles that make up this ring current come from. Two major sources are known: the solar wind, which carries charged particles outward from the Sun, and Earth's ionosphere, an electrically charged layer of the upper atmosphere. Both typically supply particles during geomagnetic storms, and some scientists expected the solar wind to remain an notable contributor during an extreme event involving particularly dense solar wind.

Instead, the first direct measurements of ring current composition during a storm of this magnitude revealed something remarkable. Particles originating from the solar wind contributed very little, while those coming from Earth's own atmosphere dominated to an extent never previously observed.

According to recent reports, published in Science Advances, the findings suggest that Earth's atmosphere may play a much greater role in determining the severity of extreme geomagnetic storms than scientists previously recognized. Because the dominant ions from Earth are much heavier than the particles supplied by the solar wind, they may have strengthened the magnetic disturbance and caused the ring current to reach its greatest intensity unusually close to the planet.

The discovery also strengthens the case for a proposed Japanese satellite mission designed to investigate how atmospheric particles enter space and influence powerful geomagnetic storms.

How the May 2024 Solar Superstorm Disrupted Earth's Magnetic Field.

According to recent reports, on May 10 and 11, 2024, enormous clouds of charged solar particles struck Earth's magnetosphere, triggering one of the most powerful geomagnetic storms in decades. Known as the "Gannon storm" or "Mother's Day storm," the event pushed the SYM-H index, a measure of geomagnetic disturbance, to a minimum of −518 nanotesla. This represented the second-largest recorded disturbance since 1981. The previous storm of comparable strength occurred in November 2004.

Although the colorful auroras drew worldwide attention, the consequences of such storms can extend far beyond the night sky.

"Some super or extreme geomagnetic storms are not just impressive light reveals -- they pose radiation risks to spacecraft, disturb GPS signals and communications, and cause power outages. Understanding how a geomagnetic storm develops is not only a scientific question, but also one with real-world consequences," mentioned Naritoshi Kitamura, lead author and designated assistant professor from the Institute for Space-Earth Environmental Research (ISEE) at Nagoya University.

It has been revealed that A major source of these magnetic disturbances is Earth's ring current. This enormous belt of energetic charged particles, primarily oxygen and hydrogen ions, slowly circulates around the planet thousands of kilometers above the equator.

In a recent development, as the ions move, they create an electrical current that generates its own magnetic field. That field partly opposes Earth's natural magnetic field, weakening the magnetic field measured at ground level. The resulting changes are among the key signals scientists use to track the strength of geomagnetic storms.

Japanese Satellite Reveals an Unexpected Source of Storm Particles.

It has been revealed that scientists were able to investigate the May 2024 storm in unusual detail thanks to Japan's Arase satellite, which was launched in 2016 and is operated by the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). The ERG (Arase) science center is jointly operated by the Institute of Space and Astronautical Science (ISAS)/JAXA and the Institute for Space-Earth Environmental Research/Nagoya University.

Arase travels through the region of space where Earth's ring current forms. Its scientific instruments can measure both the mass and energy of individual ions, allowing researchers to determine the types of particles present during a storm.

By remarkable timing, the spacecraft passed through the ring current shortly after the May 2024 storm began and again as the disturbance approached its peak. These observations provided a rare opportunity to examine the composition of the ring current during an exceptionally powerful geomagnetic event.

"This is the first simultaneous observation of ring current ions and solar wind during a storm this large, and the data was clear -- approximately 85% of ions were oxygen from Earth's own ionosphere," Kitamura explained.

Recent findings suggest that the overwhelming contribution from Earth's atmosphere was particularly surprising because the storm had been triggered by dense streams of material arriving from the Sun. Rather than supplying most of the ring current ions, the solar wind played a relatively minor role in the measured particle population.

Earth's Magnetic Field Weakened by 40%.

Sources indicate that the Arase measurements revealed another extraordinary feature of the storm. The magnetic field weakened dramatically in a region much closer to Earth than where similarly severe reductions had previously been documented.

"Near the peak of the storm, Arase detected a 40% decrease in magnetic field intensity at roughly 16,000 kilometers above Earth, and much closer to Earth than similar large decreases previously documented.".

At the same time, the satellite detected a decline in the number of energetic electrons that normally circulate through this region of space.

Industry observers note that such an extreme weakening of the magnetic field can alter the paths followed by these electrons, causing them to drift away from their usual orbits. However, scientists have not yet determined whether the deformation of the magnetic field directly caused the observed electron loss. Further research will be needed to establish that connection.

Industry observers note that together, the observations provide new insight into how the ring current behaves during especially intense geomagnetic storms. They also suggest that the unusually large population of heavy ions originating from Earth's atmosphere may have helped produce the severe magnetic disturbance so close to the planet.

A New Clue to Predicting Dangerous Solar Storms.

Industry observers note that the findings could have important implications for space weather forecasting. Current models rely heavily on conditions in the solar wind to estimate how powerful an approaching geomagnetic storm might become.

Industry observers note that however, the new measurements suggest that conditions within Earth's own upper atmosphere could also influence a storm's eventual intensity. Understanding how many atmospheric ions escape into the magnetosphere, and how they contribute to the ring current, may therefore be essential for making more reliable predictions.

The researchers believe that additional satellite observations could help answer these questions. Their findings support FACTORS, a proposed mission involving two satellites that is being prepared for an upcoming JAXA proposal opportunity.

FACTORS would investigate the processes that allow ions from Earth's atmosphere to flow into the magnetosphere and examine how those particles contribute to the development of geomagnetic storms.

By revealing how Earth's atmosphere and incoming solar material interact during extreme events, the mission could eventually improve forecasts of dangerous space weather. More accurate predictions would help scientists better anticipate storms capable of disrupting satellites, navigation systems, communications networks, and power infrastructure.

Study finds slightly higher risk of autism diagnosis in areas with more lithium in drinking water, but experts say more research is needed
