30 years ago, 'Space Jam' proposed the best way to resolve interplanetary disputes

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1217 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that you just ordered a Pizza Hut and a two-liter bottle of Mountain Dew.
  • The entire concept of "Space Jam" is so '90s that you swear you can hear Los Del Rio in the background mouthing, "Dale a tu cuerpo alegría, Macarena." As ridiculous as an intergalactic basketball match may sound, it's a perfect example of how even the strangest idea can work if you commit to it fully.
  • Sources indicate that in case you thought you hallucinated the whole thing, no, you didn't, as the Looney Tunes find themselves in quite the predicament in this live-action-animation hybrid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that you just ordered a Pizza Hut and a two-liter bottle of Mountain Dew. You put on "Space Jam" to watch the greatest of all time team up with the Looney Tunes. It's a perfect evening… in 1996 or 2026.

The entire concept of "Space Jam" is so '90s that you swear you can hear Los Del Rio in the background mouthing, "Dale a tu cuerpo alegría, Macarena." As ridiculous as an intergalactic basketball match may sound, it's a perfect example of how even the strangest idea can work if you commit to it fully.

Sources indicate that in case you thought you hallucinated the whole thing, no, you didn't, as the Looney Tunes find themselves in quite the predicament in this live-action-animation hybrid. A bunch of aliens known as the Nerdlucks arrive on Earth to abduct the Tunes and take them back as attractions to the outer-space amusement park known as Moron Mountain (shockingly nobody has claimed that subreddit, so do your thing, Internet!).

Industry observers note that being a wheeling-and-dealing wabbit, though, Bugs Bunny proposes a winner-takes-all basketball game between the Tunes and the tiny Nerdlucks. Unfortunately, the crafty aliens use their tech to steal the talent from ballers like Charles Barkley and Muggsy Bogues and turn themselves into the scary and skilled Monstars.

So, Bugs and friends reach out to Michael Jordan, who recently switched from basketball to baseball, to help the Tune Squad win this intergalactic b-ball matchup and their freedom, because if anybody can do it, Air Jordan (Hare Jordan?) can. Oh, Bill Murray also indicates up here a few times. Why? Because he can!

"Space Jam" is a spin on the classic sci-fi trope of resolving high-stakes conflicts through sports. In 1975, "Death Race 2000" introduced a world where people drive like hooligans and bash into each other to get ahead and win races (ironically, this is the regular experience on any public road now). Meanwhile, in the same year, "Rollerball" demonstrated how to use extreme sports as a plot device whereby brutality trumped any kind of skill in the arena.

Yet "Space Jam" took this concept, cartoonified it for a family-friendly audience, and challenged the conflict resolution approaches of other alien invasion movies from 1996.

Recent findings suggest that while "Independence Day" saw the heroes trying to destroy the mothership and "Mars Attacks" featured humans running away from "Ack! Ack"-ing extraterrestrials with ray guns, this film used the court to settle the score. It's an innovative way to deal with interplanetary matters, that's for sure.

Here's the thing: a basketball game is incredibly fair and puts everybody on equal footing. It isn't about who has the biggest guns or most high-tech spacecraft; it's about who can best work as a team to get a result.

Sources indicate that now, this isn't to say that the Looney Tunes and Nerdlucks ever planned on playing by the rules. Bugs challenged his opponents to a basketball contest because they were small and he knew the Tunes would have the height advantage. However, the aliens pulled a fast one by stealing b-ball talent and evolving into the brutish Monstars. Basically the cartoon version of when athletes use PEDs….

Even so, you can't argue that a basketball game gives each side a genuine chance at victory. Let's be real here for a moment: if humans were to face off against aliens in actual warfare, we would get smoked in seconds. Hell, we would probably get stuck in a tailspin of political infighting and the passing of the buck or end up destroying ourselves before the aliens even fired a single shot. On the court, though, there's no place to hide. Everybody needs to get up and slam!

In a recent development, there's also something magical about having MJ as the de facto leader of the Tune Squad. In the '90s, he was the closest thing to a real-life superhero that the world had ever seen. He broke basketball records, then headed off to another sport — baseball — to challenge himself. His love for the court never died, though, so he came back for the last dance. "Space Jam" found a clever way to blur the line between fiction and reality to elevate MJ's already iconic status.

Sure, Jordan wasn't exactly Daniel Day-Lewis in this film, but he did his best. "He did as well as he could do," director Joe Pytka told Entertainment Weekly. "He played himself, and remember, a lot of the film is based on his life, so there were realistic references there. He was very professional; he demonstrated up, he knew his lines, and we made it as easy as possible.”.

Recent findings suggest that it's this type of dedication and professionalism that turned him into the greatest of all time. If you want to debate whether that honor belongs to LeBron James, go argue with a wall. We all watched LeBron in the 2021 sequel "Space Jam: A Fresh Legacy," and let's just say that it makes "Morbius" look like "Casablanca" by comparison, and it deserves the flak it got.

Sources indicate that back with the infinitely better original "Space Jam" movie, it isn't just the courtside matchup to decide the Tunes' fate that surprises, but also the aftermath. Unlike other alien movies that see extraterrestrials being vaporized in the final act, this film demonstrates the power of humility in victory.

MJ understands that the Monstars only did the bidding of Mr. Swackhammer (voiced by the sensational Danny DeVito) and challenges them to free themselves. After the Monstars send Swackhammer packing to the moon, they befriend the Tunes, and there's good vibes all around. The beef is settled, and the only rivalry that remains is the competitive one on the court. That's all, folks!

Instead of treating the aliens as the enemy that must be destroyed, "Space Jam" looks at these creatures as misguided and simply following instructions. They aren't bad guys; they're foot soldiers. Once they break free from Swackhammer's shackles, everybody gets along. And hey, maybe Marvin the Martian also put in a good word for them.

It's a testament to the quality of "Space Jam" that everybody still talks about it 30 years later, but nobody can even remember Steven Spielberg's "Disclosure Day" from a few months ago.

In 1996, aliens were all the rage (and a little overexposed if we're being honest) but "Space Jam" still managed to find a unique and compelling angle that stood out from everything else around it. Not only that, but it also paid tribute to one of the greatest sportsmen to have ever walked the planet.

This wasn't just a slam dunk in cinema; it was boomshakalaka!

"Space Jam" is available to watch on HBO Max.

Latest Update: The Best Smart Bird Feeders for Backyard Birding (2026)

📅 19 Jul 2024 | ⏱️ 31 min read (6200 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~31 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You’ve probably seen a smart bird feeder or know someone who has one.
  • To answer these questions, I’ve been testing the most popular smart bird feeders, including models from Birdfy and Birdbuddy, for more than two years—in rain, snow, and heat, and in a yard with persistent varmints.
  • It has been revealed that updated November 2026: I’ve added the Birdbuddy Nook as a upcoming Best Budget pick, Kiwibit's Feeder 2 Pro as an Honorable Mention, and information on Birdfy's rollout of free AI ID.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You’ve probably seen a smart bird feeder or know someone who has one. The best smart bird feeders are easily recognizable with their clear housing, cameras, and solar panels. Perhaps a friend or family member has sent you a photo or video of a bright goldfinch or a handsome woodpecker (guilty). But are these feeders really worth their $100-plus price tag? Are they durable? And what about the squirrel problem?

To answer these questions, I’ve been testing the most popular smart bird feeders, including models from Birdfy and Birdbuddy, for more than two years—in rain, snow, and heat, and in a yard with persistent varmints. I’ve explored the apps and notification settings, examined the photo and video quality, noted which features are hidden behind a subscription paywall, and used Cornell Lab’s All About Birds—as well as Google Lens and my own expertise—to verify the accuracy of AI identifications. The recommendations below are what I would buy with my own money, having tested dozens of brands and models for a minimum of four weeks each.

It has been revealed that updated November 2026: I’ve added the Birdbuddy Nook as a upcoming Best Budget pick, Kiwibit's Feeder 2 Pro as an Honorable Mention, and information on Birdfy's rollout of free AI ID. I've also removed a couple of discontinued feeders and updated links and prices.

This cheery blue- or yellow-roofed feeder, from security tech giant Netvue, was the first smart feeder WIRED tested, back in 2022, when it earned a 6/10 rating due to its high price and wonky AI. Both metrics have improved dramatically since then—Birdfy's app is now the second-most user-friendly on the market, behind only Birdbuddy's, and this feeder is often on sale for around $130. Its AI identification, which is decent, used to be paywalled but is now free with every tier of feeder.

Industry observers note that the 1080p/2K camera isn't the best quality you'll find, but it does have one of the widest viewing angles of any smart feeder, at 155 degrees, so you're more likely to get full bird shots, as opposed to just heads and butts. The plastic housing (available in blue or yellow) also makes this feeder durable and easy to clean, and the 50-ounce seed reservoir is super easy to fill with its convenient flip-up top. Not all bundles come with a solar panel, but you can buy one separately. Unlike with other feeders, the solar panel is not built in and needs to be mounted and connected separately with the included 9.8-foot charging cable.

It's not the fanciest feeder on the market, nor the one with the best camera, but I've never had a problem with the two models I've been rotating in and out throughout the years, and the reliability and price point make it the best bet for most backyard birders.

Target (Solar + Extended Perch).

Birdbuddy's brand-latest Nook model is a lot of bird feeder for the price; it won our recent head-to-head test of sub-$100 smart feeders. The base $99 model doesn't come with a solar roof or extended perch, as seen in the photo above, but you will get a 2K HDR camera that can shoot vertically or horizontally (it pops in and out via a magnet), as well as the same sturdy, high-quality construction as Birdbuddy's pricier Home model. The seed capacity isn't the greatest at 0.9 liters, but the app is easy to use and can even identify birds nearby that don't land on the feeder, so long as its excellent onboard microphone hears their sounds.

Birdbuddy's Achilles’ heel has always been its sensor, which is slow to wake up and regularly misses bird visits. The latest Birdbuddy feeder supposedly has a faster wake-up time than previous models, and though it still lagged behind Birdfy's competing Rookie feeder in capturing all visits, the Nook's rate was substantially better than the Home's. It also has more mounting options, allowing for hanging in addition to wall and pole mounts (though the latter is a loose fit), and allows for no-cost manual AI ID of all visitors.

Camojojo's original Hibird feeder has long been a reliable model in my testing stable, one of the first to run on both 2.4-GHz and 5-GHz Wi-Fi bands, and last year saw the debut of an upgraded model, the Hibird Pro. The update has built-in solar panels, an option for pole-mounting, and supposedly improved AI identification, though it still frequently misidentifies even common birds in my West Coast backyard as East Coast species. The app is not as streamlined or user-friendly as Birdfy's or Birdbuddy's, but it's still easy enough to navigate, with options for changing video length (default is 10 seconds) or viewing in slo-mo. The default media type it saves is video, though this is 4K Ultra HD, and the images are—as expected—extremely sharp. Without a subscription, you can't search past videos by bird, and cloud storage is capped at 5 GB over 60 days; however, the feeder does come with a 128-GB SD card. You'll also get “smarter” chats with the app's AI Q&A function, “Dr. Bird,” and the ability to share across two devices with a subscription ($45 per year or $4 per month).

I appreciate the generous 1.5-liter seed hopper, although this, combined with the solar panel and battery, makes it extremely heavy. When filled, it tips the scales at 5 pounds, meaning that if you do pole-mount it, you will need to use both included hose clamps and wrench them tightly. I also wouldn't attempt to mount it on anything unstable, like a wobbly fence. Other original Hibird features that made it to the Pro include the little handles on the assembly screws (so you won't need any assembly tools) and the chunky plastic body. The latter was subjected to a little bit of squirrel-chewing during my test, but it still held up well.

In a recent development, the Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 is one of the most thoughtfully designed feeders on the market. You don't have to take down the whole feeder when refilling, as the 1.5-liter dual-hopper plastic seed reservoir is removable from the body. The 8-megapixel photos and 4K HD video have much better quality than you'll find from most competitors, and the components come apart for easy cleaning. I also tested the original version, which features a separate solar panel, and my only complaint was that the panel stopped charging the camera after about six weeks. This version features a built-in solar roof, which did an excellent job keeping the feeder charged during its six-week-long test, even on cloudy days. The plastic body is extremely thick and sturdy, and unlike lighter-weight feeders like Birdfy's, it's designed to hold up in more extreme weather.

The app is easy to navigate, and the whole setup is functional without a Kiwibit Plus subscription ($90/year, purchasable online or through the Kiwibit app) but you'll be losing out on a lot of features, including 60-day storage and the ability to record up to three minutes of video if a bird is doing something interesting—a unique feature among smart feeders, and one I discovered that I love. (There's nothing more frustrating than having a video cut off right as a bird is about to do something funny.) This smart feeder costs a bit much for what it is, but if you know you like having a smart feeder, I think it's worth the investment. Note, however, that it only works on 2.4-GHz Wi-Fi, and the warranty is half the length you get from many competitors. I also tested Kiwibit's newer model, the Feeder 2 Pro, and while its camera does have an interesting auto-zoom lens, I didn't think it was worth the $120 premium over this model.

Industry observers note that birdbuddy is known for its user-friendliness and thoughtful app—its Pro Smart Hummingbird Feeder is no exception. The feeder is intuitive and easy to use, and you don't need a subscription to access fun features like AI identification, 5 MP photos, and 2K HD video with slo-mo. A subscription unlocks features like family sharing and a higher bit rate, but the feeder is perfectly functional without those. With the panel being built into the feeder's roof, there’s also no auxiliary solar panel to worry about. Pairing with your phone is a cinch, integrating it into the Birdbuddy app with other feeders is a snap, and even refilling it is no problem. Unlike other hummingbird feeders that have weirdly cavernous capacities and/or need to be filled upside down, the Birdbuddy’s bottom screws off and holds a reasonable 1.75 cups of liquid. This detail is important; as the Cornell Lab of Ornithology points out, the easier it is to clean a hummingbird feeder, the more likely you are to do it often and well.

In a recent development, this feeder also comes with extra plastic flowers and a little brush for scrubbing them, and the app sends reminders when it's time to clean. You'll find fun, seasonal touches in the app, like the ability to send digital bird holiday cards with the photos your feeder captures, and a tool that superimposes hats, clothes, and various accessories on the birds, which is actually funnier than it sounds. However, as with the Birdbuddy seed feeders, the massive downside is that the feeder's sensor doesn’t always pick up every bird that visits. This can definitely be a bummer, particularly when you see something interesting out the window but it doesn’t show up in the app.

In a recent development, after experiencing connection problems with the Birdfy Polygon, I swapped it out for the newer Birdfy Nest Duo and have had no issues. The sleek, contemporary Duo is a fir box fitted with two cameras—one facing the hole and one tucked discreetly inside the feeder. That gives you a full-spectrum view of what's going on. Both cameras have night vision (the internal one is infrared). Like the Polygon, the Duo sports a remote for rebooting and recharging the camera (though the separate solar panel, which can be pole-mounted, has kept the cameras reliably charged), as well as different-size holes for different species, each with its own chew-proof predator guard.

Sources indicate that there's a metal grate with drainage holes that you can slot into grooves in the lower third of the Nest to make the cavity larger or smaller. The interested birds of my yard seemed very put off by the grate, so I covered it with a layer of craft mat moss, which was a success—a chickadee promptly moved in and laid seven eggs, all of which hatched. (I detail the experience in a separate review). For the first time, I was able to use the Birdfy app's ability to collect images from its nest boxes and string them together in a “story” that's shareable online. But I didn't find it especially useful or accurate. No matter, though, because the video captures have been a truly fascinating and educational experience, and I wish I could afford to buy the Duo for everyone I know.

Sources indicate that so far, the Duo has been rained on a bunch and survived a couple of heat waves, but the wood finish and black paint are peeling and will need refinishing before I put them up for next season. (The feeder comes equipped with a thermometer and hygrometer to keep an eye on conditions. I recently had to zip-tie an umbrella to mine during a heat wave, which likely saved some fledglings' lives, though the lightweight construction and black-painted side and top probably contributed to the box overheating.).

Sources indicate that I rarely expect (or get) compliments on my backyard smart feeders, but I have gotten many on this one, which has a distinctively modern look with natural wood (bamboo that's FSC-certified to be responsibly sourced) and a black-painted side and roof. It blends right into the landscape as opposed to providing a visual pop of plastic. (The pole and baffle shown in the photo above are not included.).

Birdfy's user-friendly app presents 2K HD images and video with free lifetime AI ID, and it's easy to share photos and videos with others. There's a solar panel you can mount separately, but I didn't do this and was impressed that the camera ran for nearly two months on an indoor USB-C charge.

According to recent reports, wood obviously comes with a higher risk of chewing by squirrels and other rodents, but there are metal guards available (both Birdfy-brand and aftermarket) that fit over the seed. I followed the 5-7-9 rule for pole-mounting to avoid this problem, but I was totally shocked at how weathered my feeder got after two months. And this was in a Pacific Northwest dry summer—about as mild as it gets. The finish was completely peeling off, so I recommend adding an extra layer of urethane (this is what I use) before putting it out for the first time, especially now, heading into winter.

Kiwibit’s latest upgrade to its original Feeder 2 is an interesting one; it’s the first bird feeder camera to feature autofocus in 4K HDR. The quality was exceptional, though, during my testing, some birds were alarmed by the camera movement. The biggest downside, though, is that most of this feeder’s features—including AI bird identification, expanded gallery views, and 60-day cloud storage—are now locked behind a $90-a-year paywall. It's not enough of an upgrade to justify paying the extra cash over the base-model Bird Feeder 2.

Sources indicate that A lower-maintenance way to enjoy birds in your yard, this recycled-plastic birdbath comes outfitted with a dual-lens camera sending 1080p photos and 2K video via the Birdfy app and using the app’s AI capability for (free) bird identification. With the IP66-rated birdbath’s sturdy metal base (you can buy it for less without) and solar-powered battery and fountain pump, all you have to do is make sure the 3.5-liter, 1.65-inch reservoir is topped off with water. I've been using the Bath Pro for two seasons now, and while early connection problems have been resolved, the plastic has weathered, and the pump only works intermittently. I also find myself increasingly irritated with how long footage takes to load and how often the shallow plastic basin needs refilling and cleaning—every two or three days in dry weather. Still, if you're willing to put up with some quirks, the Bath Pro has been an entertaining and welcome addition to my bird-feeding setup.

Recent findings suggest that how was test unit obtained? Press sample from organization Where is it now? In my yard.

In a recent development, birdfy's unique flagship upgrade for 2025 won a CES Innovation Award and an American Good Design Gold Award. It features one dual-lens front-facing camera (2-MP/1080p wide-angle and 3-MP/2K portrait) and one 2-MP/1080p side camera. Both capture sharp, highly detailed video with high-quality sound. The front-facing camera even pans and crops to ensure the lens is focused on a bird. (Note that there's also a cheaper, single-camera version of the Feeder 2 that we haven't tested.) The feeder's IP66-rated plastic body, which has held up very well in Pacific Northwest winter weather, is wall-, pole-, or tree-mountable. An auxiliary solar panel and lifetime AI bird identification are both included. The reservoir holds slightly less seed than the original plastic Birdfy, at 42 ounces versus Birdfy 1’s 50 ounces. Overall, I was impressed with both the image quality and the Birdfy app's updated AI identification. That said, both cameras repeatedly dropped connections during my two-month testing period, even though I was using the required 2.4-GHz Wi-Fi network (only the Birdfy Metal 2 can run on 5 GHz). The solar panel, which requires separate mounting, also failed to keep the cameras consistently charged in cloudy weather.

It has been revealed that how was test unit obtained? Press sample from organization Where is it now? Office storage.

In a recent development, this Kiwibit is thoughtfully designed, with a plastic seed reservoir that's removable from the body for refilling, so you don't have to take down the whole thing. What to Look for When Buying a Smart Bird Feeder.

Industry observers note that the world of smart bird feeders is vast and can seem overwhelming, but there are some key features that will really make a difference in your user experience. I've tested dozens of feeders for years from many different brands, and this is what I think you should pay attention to when comparing models.

Subscription: Most, if not all, smart bird feeders require a subscription to access all features. That's in order to support the tech giant's continued investment in user experience. There are few things more disappointing than giving or receiving a smart bird feeder as a gift, only to find out it's not actually usable without shelling out an additional $70 a year. Reputable companies will note subscription requirements up front, and some even offer models that have a lifetime subscription built in. Note that if a feeder costs less than a hundred bucks, odds are it will require a subscription to capture photos, whether it states so in the marketing materials or not. You will need to do your due diligence before buying.

Mounting options: If you live in an area with squirrels, your best bet is to pole-mount your bird feeder—especially a more expensive smart feeder, which often has cords that squirrels and other rodents like to chew. Not all feeders offer a pole-mounting option, though, which is another important detail to confirm before buying.

Industry observers note that wi-Fi network: The vast majority of smart feeders only work on 2.4-GHz Wi-Fi frequencies. If you only use 5 GHz, you will need to look for a feeder that specifically works with a shorter transmission range or has dual range, such as the Camojojo Hibird, above.

Sources indicate that app: An app can make or break your smart bird feeder experience since it's where all of your bird viewing, sorting, and saving will take place. Apps with added features like useful facts, the capacity to share feeds with others, quality AI identification, and the ability to sort by bird are sometimes worth the added cost over a less-expensive feeder. Many companies use security cameras in their bird feeders that don't have a separate app—this means you'll just get a utilitarian list of image captures with no detail or context. To help buyers with their decision-making, I am right now building a rubric to grade and rank smart bird feeder apps, which I hope to add to this guide within the next couple of months.

How Does WIRED Test Bird Feeders?

It has been revealed that I test all feeders in my rural-suburban backyard in the Pacific Northwest. I mount seed feeders on a 1-inch pole with a baffle, using the provided mounting hardware and hose clamps. If pole-mounting isn't feasible, I mount on a fence or a shepherd's hook. I hang hummingbird feeders from a shepherd's hook mounted on the side of my house. I fill the seed feeders with Audubon Wild Park bird seed and the hummingbird feeders with a nectar mixture of 4-to-1 granulated sugar and water. I keep each feeder up for a minimum of four weeks, with all app notifications enabled.

In a recent development, I look at all app features available both with a subscription and without, seeing how often I get notifications and noting whether they are accurately picking up just birds or any type of outdoor movement, and how well the AI feature is able to distinguish bird species. I also look at connectivity, seed capacity, video quality, and how well the feeder bodies hold up to squirrels and inclement weather.

The majority of feeders I tested were provided as press samples by the manufacturer. I keep some for longer-term testing, put others in storage for future testing or comparison purposes, and donate others locally via the Buy Nothing Project.

What Do I Need to Know Before Setting Up a Smart Feeder?

Why Do Most Smart Feeders Only Run on 2.4 GHz?

This section was inspired by an email from a reader who installs home Wi-Fi systems and did not appreciate my recommending a feeder that has the option to run on 5 GHz. He's not wrong that this isn't the preferred band for a smart bird feeder, but I'll explain why someone might want 5 GHz below.

First off, what is 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz? In simplest terms, these are the main radio frequency bands Wi-Fi uses to send data wirelessly between your smart bird feeder and your router. One gigahertz (GHz) is 1 billion hertz, the unit of measurement for how fast radio waves oscillate. Both bands are the accepted standards for Wi-Fi, which yes, is a name brand.

It follows, then, that 2.4-GHz waves oscillate more slowly than 5-GHz waves. This also means the slower waves can travel farther and pass through walls and other obstacles more effectively. With Wi-Fi-enabled products placed outside the home, the ability to penetrate walls, trees, and other potential barriers is more vital than speed. These slower waves also result in less power consumption by devices. It makes sense that 2.4 GHz would be a preferable band for a smart bird feeder, which likely would be in or near a tree-filled area.

However, 2.4 GHz is a more crowded band and thus prone to interference from other Wi-Fi networks and devices, so it can be less stable. It also results in slower overall performance, leading to sluggish downloads and lag during streaming and video calls. Most modern routers offer both 2.4-GHz and 5-GHz bands, but some may be configured (for whatever reason) to broadcast only 5 GHz. Other routers feature something called band steering, which automatically diverts devices to the less-crowded 5 GHz. A smart bird feeder that offers dual connectivity simply provides more options. If the bird feeder is right outside your window where the router is located, you may want the faster speed. Or maybe you just don't want to try to figure out how to turn off band steering. If you're not dialed in to your router, no pun intended, it may make sense for you to consider a bird feeder with dual-band connectivity.

As is the case with any bird feeder, squirrels love to eat at smart bird feeders, most of which are not squirrel-proof, regardless of marketing claims. However, most of the smart feeders we’ve tested are just as sturdy, if not in some cases sturdier, than analog bird feeders. The worst-case scenario is likely the squirrel eating all the seed, chewing the edges, and covering up the camera with its fuzzy butt.

In a recent development, the yard where I test smart feeders year-round is lousy with the large and persistent rodents, and the squirrel damage I’ve sustained on test feeders has been minor. With the Birdfy Pro Duo, above, the animals chewed off the edges to better get at the seed supply when it was low, and the FeatherSnap Scout had its mounting bent. Top of mind is the 5-7-9 method of siting a bird feeder—at least 5 feet off the ground, at least 7 feet away from any structures, and at least 9 feet away from anything a squirrel could jump from (branches, fences, roofs). I explain this in more detail in my guide to keeping squirrels away from your bird feeder.

It has been revealed that another option is an aftermarket baffle added to feeders hanging on shepherd’s hooks, or a pole with a built-in baffle, like this one from Birdfy. Or you could use seed treated with capsaicin, or hot pepper. The taste doesn't affect birds, since they don’t have capsaicin receptors like mammals do. That stated, I’ve found capsaicin only keeps squirrels away for a couple of days, whether because they’ve gotten used to it or the pepper loses its potency when exposed to the elements. As a last resort, you could always just learn to live with the squirrels and dedicate a feeder to them, although my neighbor does this, and I'm of the mind that doing so brings even more squirrels to the area.

Scientists capture electrons making seemingly impossible quantum jumps

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Physicists have captured an extraordinary quantum phenomenon in which electrons appear to leap across energy gaps that would normally be off limits.
  • The effect is similar to stepping into an elevator and watching the floor display change from "1," "2," and "3" directly to "20." Instead of traveling through the seventeen floors in between, you somehow arrive at the twentieth floor.
  • Recent findings suggest that these unusual events are known as Landau-Zener-Majorana transitions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Physicists have captured an extraordinary quantum phenomenon in which electrons appear to leap across energy gaps that would normally be off limits. Using a new type of slow-motion electron camera, researchers were able to watch these incredibly fast movements in graphene, revealing how powerful electric fields can drive electrons between different energy states.

The effect is similar to stepping into an elevator and watching the floor display change from "1," "2," and "3" directly to "20." Instead of traveling through the seventeen floors in between, you somehow arrive at the twentieth floor. Although this sounds impossible in everyday life, electrons can make comparable jumps in the quantum world.

Recent findings suggest that these unusual events are known as Landau-Zener-Majorana transitions. Physicists have long suspected that they could become increasingly vital in high-speed semiconductor electronics, but observing exactly how they unfold has been a major challenge.

According to recent reports, now, researchers from the University of Regensburg, Philipps-Universität Marburg, and Forschungszentrum Jülich have directly tracked these transitions in graphene, a material made from an extremely thin layer of carbon atoms. Their findings, published in Nature, provide a detailed look at how electrons respond to intense electric fields generated by light.

How Electrons Cross Forbidden Energy Gaps.

In a recent development, in semiconductors and similar materials, electrons are restricted to particular ranges of energy called energy bands. Between these bands are regions known as forbidden energy gaps, where electrons cannot ordinarily occupy stable states.

Under normal conditions, electrons tend to remain within their existing energy bands. However, the researchers observed something very different when they exposed graphene to intense pulses of light. The electric field accelerated the electrons and caused some of them to switch from one energy band to another, crossing the intervening gap through a quantum mechanical transition.

To capture these movements, the scientists developed an experimental technique that combines advanced laser technology with electron microscopy. This allowed them to examine electron behavior on timescales far too short for conventional imaging methods.

A Slow-Motion Camera Reveals Quantum Jumps.

Sources indicate that "If you want to know who has won a race, you have to watch all participants," explains Vincent Eggers, first author of the study. "Likewise, we must observe as many electrons as possible at one time to catch those that undergo a quantum mechanical transition while moving.".

Recent findings suggest that the key instrument is a photoemission momentum microscope. Rather than producing an enlarged picture of a material's surface, as a traditional microscope would, it measures the energies of electrons and how they are moving. Researchers then use this information to create detailed maps showing how electrons are distributed across different energy states.

In a recent development, one of the biggest technical obstacles was combining these measurements with powerful light fields that oscillate at extremely high speeds. The team needed to drive the electrons into motion while simultaneously recording how their energies and movements changed.

Sources indicate that "Our team worked on this experiment for many years. Now, we can track electrons moving across the entire energy landscape of a solid in real time," indicates Rupert Huber.

Ulrich Höfer, a collaborator on the project and a pioneer in ultrafast electron spectroscopy, describes the excitement of witnessing the effect firsthand.

"Being able to observe such a fundamental quantum mechanical process during our first measurement campaign was a very special moment for us - it was also made possible by the samples we used.".

Ultra-Pure Graphene Makes the Discovery Possible.

The experiment depended on exceptionally pure graphene samples manufactured at Forschungszentrum Jülich. These specially prepared carbon layers were only one atom thick and had to be nearly flawless for the measurements to work.

"These precision experiments require material that is nearly perfect at the atomic level. This ensures that impurities do not obscure the delicate quantum dynamics of the electrons. Another crucial factor for the study was the use of "rotated" graphene, a specialty from Jülich, which allows the quantum dynamics to emerge particularly clearly," emphasizes Stefan Tautz from Forschungszentrum Jülich.

The carefully engineered material made it possible to distinguish the delicate quantum effects from interference caused by imperfections in the graphene.

According to recent reports, what the researchers saw was remarkable. When exposed to sufficiently strong light fields, electrons crossed the forbidden energy gap with a transition probability reaching 100 percent.

Sources indicate that this result highlights one of the most surprising features of Landau-Zener-Majorana transitions. Electrons can move between energy states with very high probability even when those states are separated by a substantial energy gap.

The crucial factor is how promptly the electrons approach the gap under the influence of the electric field. This makes the process fundamentally different from conventional quantum tunneling, in which particles pass through a barrier in physical space.

A New Path Toward Light-Controlled Electronics.

Beyond revealing a fundamental quantum phenomenon, the upcoming imaging technique could help scientists understand what prevents electrons from moving in a controlled and predictable way.

Recent findings suggest that the graphene experiments have already provided an important clue. Although the electrons initially move in an orderly fashion, their interactions with the material's crystal lattice gradually disrupt that motion. Understanding these effects could help researchers develop more precise ways to control electron behavior.

Industry observers note that this knowledge is particularly valuable for future electronic technologies that could use the extremely rapid oscillations of light to direct electrons instead of relying entirely on electrical voltages. Such approaches could open fresh possibilities for manipulating electronic properties at exceptionally high speeds.

The researchers also expect their method to work with many other quantum materials, allowing scientists to investigate previously inaccessible electron dynamics and potentially discover new ways to control them.

As Giacomo Inzani from the University of Regensburg explains, the achievement marks the beginning of a much broader exploration.

"Our experiment opens a panoramic window into the quantum world. Now, we can follow in real time how electrons move through the energy landscape of a material. And this is just the beginning. Our method can be applied to many other quantum materials, opening up completely upcoming possibilities for controlling their electronic properties selectively with light.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ta-Nehisi Coates, Kamilah Forbes and Kenyatta Matthews are formally announcing their organization, Maceo-Lyn Productions, with the premiere of the HBO Original documentary When A Witness Recants.

The documentary, which airs Nov. 17, is one of several projects at the production company, including the upcoming feature film adaptation of The Water Dancer, the debut novel from Coates. Forbes is also directing the Broadway play Mix and Master, starring Tony Award winners Kara Young and Ruben Santiago-Hudson, in January 2027, as well as Boom for Real, a fresh musical in development about Jean-Michel Basquiat with a score by John Legend.

It has been revealed that the company was formed in 2020, with the documentary film adaptation of Coates’ Between the World and Me, as their first project. Forbes directed the film, and helmed the prior stage adaptation.

While Coates mentioned he didn’t set out to create a production company (“I actually wanted nothing to do with Hollywood at all,” Coates said), he valued working with close collaborators on the project. Matthews and Forbes became friends in middle school, and then met Coates at Howard University, with Matthews later marrying Coates.

“I think there was a level of trust between the three of us, and it was quite clear that we probably would continue to work in that space after this, even though it wasn’t a thing I necessarily saw for myself. I just did not want to be in business with people who I did not have a deep understanding of, and who did not have a deep understanding of me, both aesthetically and ideologically,” Coates told The Hollywood Reporter.

Forbes, former executive producer at the Apollo, notes that they’re prioritizing quality over quantity, with the projects meant to appeal to their varied backgrounds in journalism and writing, theater, as well as social activism, with a focus on Black storytelling and moving the culture forward.

It has been revealed that “I think it comes to what’s moving us?” Forbes said. “I think our partnership is really unique simply because we come to storytelling from several different corners.”.

Sources indicate that “What moves the needle for us. What are the stories that we’re just haunted by?,” added Matthews. In the case of When A Witness Recants, which follows the wrongful murder conviction of three Baltimore teenagers, Matthews notes that she became fixated on the story after staying up late reading the 2021 Fresh Yorker article. Coates, who grew up in the same neighborhood, had been similarly fixated by the case.

Future work is expected to span across film, television and theater, scripted and non-scripted, with the trio teasing an upcoming documentary about historical figures.

“One of the things that we really do prize at Maceo-Lyn, we value words. I mean, we can’t not with Ta-Nehisi being one of the three prongs of the company, and so we always start with what is the written piece that moves us. Be it a script, be it a magazine article, be it a play,” Matthews stated.

Coates noted that he is excited to see the feature film adaptation of his debut novel, about a man born into slavery with the power to transport himself long distances, which has been in the works since 2019 with Brad Pitt’s Blueprint B.

It has been revealed that “There’s been some changes in the industry that presented some challenges, but I think nonetheless both Kenyatta and Kamilah and our partners over at Initiative B, we’re really excited about bringing that to film. It’s one of these things where you can’t get it wrong. I mean, something about making a bad slavery film is significantly worse than just making a bad film,” Coates stated.

Simon Robinson, one of the fans who traveled to Bangkok for the Eurovision Song Contest on Saturday, stated that his history with the competition is nearly as long as its seven-decade run.

He was eight years old when he first watched it with his family in Yorkshire, England, when Britain's Mary Hopkin finished in second place behind Ireland’s Dana.

Recent findings suggest that “I really liked the concept of bringing Europe together after the war,” said Mr. Robinson, 63, who now lives in Melbourne, Australia. He described the contest’s annual broadcast as a social activity for his family and neighbors.

“Eurovision helped to create the European identity,” he added.

Other fans had their own motivations for traveling to see the contest’s first Asian edition.

Some are Europeans living in Asia, on the hunt for nostalgia, while others are Americans who were eager to experience their first Eurovision.

Lee Hudson, an American television executive based in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, mentioned that he gets emotional when he talks about Eurovision, which he has watched since 2012.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that editor’s Note:  Call to Earth is a CNN editorial series committed to reporting on the environmental challenges facing our planet, together with the solutions. Rolex’s Perpetual Planet initiative has partnered with CNN to drive awareness and education around key sustainability issues and to inspire positive action.

Originally a term used by trophy hunters in Africa, the “Big Five” described the animals most challenging to shoot and kill: the lion, elephant, leopard, rhino, and buffalo. Nowadays, it is more loosely used to refer to some of Africa’s largest and most iconic animals.

In a recent development, however, British photographer Graeme Green has reclaimed the narrative, creating a global “Latest Major Five” for wildlife photography. In 2021, 50,000 people around the world voted for the five animals they would most like to photograph, or see photographed, in the wild. Five animals were crowned the winners: the elephant, polar bear, lion, gorilla and tiger.

This week, sees the publication of “The Latest Significant 5” photography book, which features images of those animals and other at-risk wildlife, from photography legends such as Ami Vitale, Steve McCurry and Paul Nicklen, and essays from famous conservationists and activists including like Jane Goodall and Paula Kahumbu.

Green indicates that the book celebrates wildlife and is a global call to action on issues impacting wildlife, including habitat loss, poaching, pollution and climate change.

Green was on assignment in Botswana at least a decade ago when he came up with the idea for a project to encourage people to “shoot with a camera, not a gun,” he says.

“I thought this would be a way to get people really focusing on wildlife, thinking about the wildlife they love, thinking about the animals that are at risk.”.

Ten photographs that made the world wake up to climate change.

In total, the book includes the work of 144 globally renowned wildlife photographers from Ecuador to India. Curating the images took nearly two years of work, states Green.

“I think these are some of the most beautiful and creative images that I’ve seen put together in one book,” indicates Green. “These are the species that we are at risk of losing.”.

In a recent development, according to the UN, nature is declining at an unprecedented rate, with around one million of the planet’s animal and plant species facing extinction. The “Newly introduced Big 5,” all of which are threatened, act as ambassadors for what is happening in the natural world, claims Green.

As well as being a powerful reminder of what we stand to lose, the book also points people towards potential solutions. Featured essays explore the benefits of rewilding and the importance of indigenous communities in conservation.

A chapter on endangered species from bees to blue whales illustrates the alarming threat climate change poses to animals outside of the “Newly introduced Significant 5.” “That’s only the tip of the iceberg – I could have included thousands of pictures because that’s how serious the situation is,” says Green.

Why a wildlife photographer took 40,000 photos to capture these extraordinary birds.

Jane Goodall, a leading conservationist who also wrote the afterword to the book, said in a press release that “we have a window of time during which we can start to heal some of the harm we have inflicted on the natural world, but only if we get together and take action now.

Sources indicate that “I hope the photos will lead people into the wonderful worlds of these iconic species. Then, perhaps, other people will become involved in helping to create a world where wildlife can flourish for future generations to enjoy,” she said.

“The Newly introduced Big 5: A Global Photography Project For Endangered Wildlife,” by Graeme Green, published by Earth Aware Editions, is on sale from April 4, 2023.

This story has been updated to reflect the range of challenges covered by the book.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, to help solve this problem, Thomas A.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that fossils provide an extraordinary window into Earth's distant past, revealing the animals, plants, and ecosystems that existed millions of years ago. Yet the fossil record tells only part of the story. Fossilization is exceptionally rare, meaning that just a tiny fraction of the organisms that once lived on Earth have been preserved. Even when fossils survive, scientists can only discover them if the rock layers containing them are accessible today.

As a result, our picture of prehistoric life is filled with major gaps. Some geological periods and parts of the world have produced abundant fossils, giving scientists a detailed understanding of the life that existed there. Other periods and regions remain largely unexplored. Because fossil excavations require considerable time and resources, knowing where to search could make a major difference in uncovering new evidence of ancient life.

In a recent development, to help solve this problem, Thomas A. Neubauer of the Bavarian State Collections of Natural History (SNSB) and Mathias Harzhauser of the Natural History Museum in Vienna have developed a new tool for guiding fossil research. The two paleontologists analyzed the geographic distribution of fossil discoveries from animals that inhabited shallow marine environments over the past 540 million years. For the first time, they also mapped the regions of the world where fossil information is missing, providing a clearer picture of where future discoveries may be possible.

Mapping 540 Million Years of Ancient Marine Life.

Recent findings suggest that to build their map, the researchers examined records from the Paleobiology Database (PBDB), the world's leading freely accessible repository of fossil information. The database contains a substantial portion of the paleontological findings published by scientists around the world.

Sources indicate that using these records, the team reconstructed where fossils from ancient shallow marine environments have been documented throughout Earth's history. They also examined how fossil research has developed over decades and centuries, measuring how frequently investigations in different regions have produced new scientific information.

In a recent development, the researchers then compared these findings with geological information from the Macrostat database. This allowed them to assess not only where fossils have already been discovered, but also where suitable rock formations could provide opportunities to fill important gaps in the fossil record.

Where Earth's Missing Fossils May Be Hiding.

The analysis revealed a surprising imbalance in our understanding of prehistoric life. The Early Mesozoic (approx. 252 to 66 million years ago) and the Palaeozoic (approx. 539 to 252 million years ago) have already been studied extensively. According to the researchers, additional fossil discoveries from these periods are unlikely to produce a substantial increase in scientific knowledge in the near future.

The greatest opportunities for expanding the fossil record may instead lie in more recent geological history. Although scientists have already collected extensive evidence from the Cenozoic Era (beginning 66 million years ago), the analysis suggests that its shallow marine deposits still contain significant untapped potential for fossil discoveries.

Industry observers note that to help researchers investigate this period, the team identified locations around the world where previously unknown fossil species are especially likely to be found. Crucially, these are also places where the appropriate geological layers are exposed or otherwise accessible, making actual discoveries possible.

A Treasure Map for Future Fossil Discoveries.

By highlighting regions where key evidence may still be waiting, the new approach could help paleontologists blueprint more productive expeditions and make better use of limited research resources. Rather than concentrating on areas that have already been explored extensively, scientists can focus on locations with the greatest potential to reveal something new about Earth's prehistoric ecosystems.

"The fact that many regions of the Earth remain unexplored offers hope for valuable new discoveries," indicates SNSB paleobiologist Neubauer.

"But precisely because expanding the fossil record is quite challenging and progresses only slowly, our work can help researchers worldwide to focus their research specifically on these still largely unexplored areas. We provide a valuable guide for planning future projects and excavation campaigns. The same applies to the examination of existing museum collections awaiting scientific analysis. Through sensible prioritization, we can fill gaps in the fossil record strategically.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the sixth movie in the $3.3 billion Hunger Games franchise contends, like many series entries before it, with a somewhat jarring tonal discordancy between the glitzy spectacle and grotesque political satire of the Capitol and the emotionally loaded brutality of the Arena, where children and teens from each of the 12 districts of Panem are forced to fight for their lives until only one is standing. But Sunrise on the Reaping overcomes that imbalance because the horror of the survival battle and the sorrow of the losses sustained are rendered with as much scalding pathos as suspense and excitement. Related Stories Movies Dual Oscar Winner Christopher Hampton Calls Glenn Close Honorary Oscar "the Least They Can Do," Says AI Is Just "a Super Google" Movies Governors Awards: Glenn Close, Ridley Scott and Floyd Norman Accept Honorary Oscars, Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler Receive Thalberg Award.

Francis Lawrence, who has directed all but the first of the features adapted from Suzanne Collins’ hugely popular YA novels, knows what he’s doing. But the surprise asset here is Australian actor Joseph Zada in a breakout performance as 16-year-old Haymitch Abernathy, the rebellious victor of the 50th Hunger Games. The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping The Bottom Line Delivers on emotion and brutal spectacle. Release date: Friday, Nov. 20Cast: Joseph Zada, Jesse Plemons, Ralph Fiennes, Glenn Close, Kieran Culkin, Elle Fanning, Mckenna Grace, Maya Hawke, Whitney Peak, Kelvin Harrison Jr., Ben Wang, Billy Porter, Molly McCann, Iona Bell, Lili Taylor, Percy Daggs IV, Iris Apatow, Edvyn Ryding, Jhaleil Swaby, Laura Marcus, Scot GreenanDirector: Francis LawrenceScreenwriters: Billy Ray, Michael Lesslie, based on the novel by Suzanne Collins Rated PG-13, 2 hours 43 minutes.

Played as an adult by Woody Harrelson in the first four films, Haymitch was subsequently forced to serve as a mentor to contestants every year but remained furtively on the side of the resistance. Zada (seen recently as Cal on Netflix’s East of Eden) doesn’t have much physical resemblance to Harrelson, but the voice is convincingly that of the Haymitch we know, coming into manhood with firm convictions born out of injustice and providing a resonant link to the earlier films.

Invested with tenacity, kindness and heartrending vulnerability by Zada, Haymitch provides a much more poignant and involving origin story than that of Coriolanus Snow in the lumbering first prequel, The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes. The autocratic Capitol leader would go on to consolidate his power by using the televised Games to keep the Panem population scared and under control.

Sources indicate that set 40 years after Songbirds and Snakes and 24 years before the first Hunger Games movie, Sunrise on the Reaping opens on Haymitch’s 16th birthday, which coincides with the second Quarter Quell, when the names of “tributes” from each district are drawn to enter the Arena. Being a special edition that happens just once every 25 years, the traditional choice of one male and one female has been doubled to two of each.

It has been revealed that haymitch initially is not among the four selected tributes for District 12, the grimly industrial coal mining sector where everyone appears to be living on or below the poverty line. But when one of the chosen boys tries to make a run for it and is shot by the Stormtrooper-like “Peacekeepers,” Haymitch is drawn into a skirmish and dropped into the vacant slot as punishment.

The showbiz cynicism of the operation is illustrated by Plutarch Heavensbee — Jesse Plemons in the role previously played by Philip Seymour Hoffman as an older man, following his promotion to Head Gamekeeper. Designated by the Capitol to oversee the nationwide broadcast, Plutarch dashes about giving camera directions and insisting on do-overs to maximize the drama of tributes being painfully separated from their loved ones and ushered off to almost certain death. As in the propaganda films of most dictatorial regimes, the heavily edited televised content removes all signs of messy rebellion and anti-Capitol sentiment.

The separation is especially wrenching for Haymitch from his widowed mother and adoring younger brother, but equally or perhaps even more so from his girlfriend Lenore Dove Baird (Whitney Peak), who tends geese on her father’s farm. (She’s a descendant of Lucy Gray Baird, the winner of the 10th Hunger Games, played by Rachel Zegler in Songbirds and Snakes.).

In a recent development, the sobriety of the farewells, however, is undercut by the unrestrained caricatures of some high-ranking Capitol officials. Every time the movie lurches into high-camp excess it lessens the emotional weight. The most intrusive example is Glenn Close, exploring upcoming frontiers for over-the-top as Drusilla Sickle, her contemptuous cruelty fueled by her indignation over being assigned to chaperone the District 12 tributes, whom she regards as grimy subhumans.

According to recent reports, wheeled out onstage like Hannibal Lecter to draw the lottery, Drusilla is trussed up in what looks like a leather bumblebee costume, with a red Aunt Gladys wig topped by a raven fascinator, crazy-lady makeup and a mouthful of prosthetic dentures that even Tilda Swinton might balk at. All the better to chomp on the scenery. Shrieking like a pantomime dame, Close goes full Norma Desmond and then flips to Joan Crawford mode, losing her shit with a riding crop (see 1955’s Queen Bee) when she’s sassed by Haymitch’s smart-mouthed fellow tribute Maysilee (Mckenna Grace), a shopkeeper’s daughter.

Even higher on the shrill scale is Drusilla’s husband, Capitol stylist Magno Stift (Billy Porter), sashaying around in extravagant finery with tiny live golden snakes as earrings. He declines to dress the District 12 unfortunates, sharing his lunatic wife’s opinion that they are not fit for couture. Mercifully, Magno is not around for long, making way for the familiar figure of Effie Trinket (Elle Fanning, amusingly playing a younger version of the character originated onscreen by Elizabeth Banks). The future chaperone briskly takes charge of 12’s tributes, giving their outfits an elegant upgrade before the opening ceremony chariot parade.

Recent findings suggest that while Fanning gives Effie a shot of humanity beneath her giddy glam manner, the same cannot be said of Kieran Culkin as preening TV broadcast host Caesar Flickerman. “Look alive, children, while you still can!” he tells the tributes in a bit of gallows humor that might have been funny had he not been so obnoxiously glib. Where Stanley Tucci offset Caesar’s callous showmanship with mischievous charisma in the first films, Culkin just plays sarcastic mockery. His Caesar is a charmless creep.

While the sinister combination of razzle-dazzle and fascist barbarity has always been essential to the Hunger Games world, it’s a relief here when the Capitol monsters take a backseat to the young people whose lives hang in the balance. From the very beginning, we see what a beloved figure Haymitch is in the village, how pure is the love he shares with Lenore and how tender and reassuring he is with the youngest of the district’s tributes, Louella (Molly McCann).

Recent findings suggest that they make a pact to be allies, extending also to Maysilee and fourth District 12 tribute Wyatt (Ben Wang), even if his sideline as an oddsmaker on the Games earns him some initial distrust. But when tragedy strikes early on during the chariot parade, Haymitch stares down Coriolanus Snow, his eyes expressing fury, disgust and defiance. While that uneasy moment will be cut for the broadcast, it was witnessed by the public at the opening ceremony, an embarassment to Snow that puts a target on Haymitch’s back.

Played as a youth by Tom Blyth in Songbirds and Snakes and by Donald Sutherland as an older man in the original Hunger Games quadrilogy, Snow here has the soft-spoken menace and steely authority of Ralph Fiennes. His intelligence is unquestionable but he’s also paranoid and gullible about his consigliere Plutarch and given to fits of petulant rage.

The certainty that Snow will ensure he dies an agonizing death in the Arena makes Haymitch rethink his alliances, telling the other District 12 tributes that it’s not safe to be around him. But he does enter cautiously into a pact with Ampert (Percy Daggs IV) from District 3, who informs him that other districts are open to collaboration in order to prevail over the elite contestants from Districts 1 and 2. Known as Career tributes, these are the most frequent victors in the Games, due to their wealth, privilege and extensive combat and weaponry training.

Ampert was entered into the games by Snow in retaliation for the attempt to sabotage Capitol communications by the boy’s father, Beetee (Kelvin Harrison Jr.), now forced to serve as a mentor but still secretly plotting. The mentors specifically assigned to District 12 are past victors Wiress (Maya Hawke) and Mags (Lili Taylor); neither actor is given a lot to do but they are a welcome presence — warm, supportive and candid with the tributes.

Lawrence and screenwriters Billy Ray and Michael Lesslie have relatively little time and breathing room to give the more ruthless Arena opponents much character definition. But two District 1 Careers are memorably lethal — Silka (Laura Marcus) with her double-headed axes and muscle-bound Panache (Jhaleil Swaby) with his ferocious anger and strength.

The nail-biting Arena action is vicious and bloody, sustaining high stakes as Haymitch attempts to break the Capitol’s brain hub, which sends in “mutts” — genetically modified animals, from electrified butterflies to killer squirrels and birds — to overwhelm the tributes earmarked for death.

Zada is the beating heart of the film, mutinous but neither cocky nor fearless, and he has stirring scenes with Ampert and Maysilee. The hair from one of Britney Spears’ blonde bangs periods is a distraction, but Grace is fiery in the latter role — gutsy, determined and a loyal friend to Haymitch once their allegiance is cemented. She’s also handy with a poisoned blow dart. Iona Bell as a young substitute tribute drugged into compliance by the Capitol also has touching moments.

Other cast standouts are Peak, lovely as Haymitch’s sweetheart; and the always dependable Plemons, who deftly navigates Plutarch’s double duty as a Capitol official playing for the other side.

In a recent development, bolstered by DP Jo Willems’ muscular camerawork, James Newton Howard’s soaring score and Uli Hanisch’s imaginative production design, Sunrise on the Reaping is a return, after the disappointing Songbirds and Snakes, to the spirit of the first movies. There’s even a brief appearance by baby Katniss Everdeen to complete the circle. It’s impossible not to feel sympathy when young people are being sacrificed in horrific ways for the ritualistic entertainment of the masses and the power-flexing of a pitiless overlord. A moving coda set many years later re-introduces familiar faces that will add to the satisfaction for longtime franchise fans.

Sources indicate that for 33 years, Nvidia had only one CEO. Now, just days after the chipmaker announced Jensen Huang's resignation, some of the country's biggest names are already want him back — from OpenAI CEO Sam Altman to President Donald Trump.

The decision ultimately belongs to Nvidia's board, which has appointed longtime finance chief Colette Kress as interim CEO.

Industry observers note that the calls for a comeback follow a week of mounting scrutiny over Huang's intimate extracurriculars. On Nov. 8, Huang had told employees he’d been unfaithful to his wife after reports of a relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing organization that buys Nvidia chips. U.S. officials suspect she had ties to Chinese intelligence, an allegation Beijing has denied. The same day Huang emailed employees, Nvidia's board confirmed an independent investigation into reports that he had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort. Reuters also reported that Huang had relationships with two Nvidia employees, including one who reported directly to him. Inhales.

It's a lot. But that doesn't mean everyone thinks its enough to get rid of the co-founder permanently. On Nov. 15, Huang was already talking to people close to him about a possible return, according to the Financial Times. One ally told the paper they were getting tech executives together to lobby for his reinstatement and would seek support from the White House.

In a recent development, on Monday, Trump gave that effort some encouragement. "I would certainly not mind seeing that," he told reporters before leaving Washington for the Philippines and China. He mentioned he thought Huang had "learned a major lesson" and questioned whether Alice Huang had worked for Chinese intelligence.

A day earlier, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Larry Kudlow on Fox News that Nvidia should hire its next CEO from outside the organization, saying it needed a "dramatic shake-up.".

Huang's supporters are also making their case online. "Thirty-three years deserve an answer," reads the Stand With Jensen petition, which demands that Nvidia's board reinstate its co-founder while the independent investigation is underway. "We are concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process," it adds. If directors think Huang should stay out of the job, the letter asks them to explain what evidence led them to that decision and why it serves Nvidia's interests. It also calls on the board to disclose what the investigation will cover, when it expects to finish, and how Huang will get a chance to respond. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Voyager 1 is celebrating a big milestone as it approaches its 50th birthday: reaching one light-day away from Earth.

Sources indicate that NASA's long-running interstellar Voyager 1 probe will mark one light-day of distance from Earth on Nov. 18, when the spacecraft is 49 years, two months and 11 days old. The agency recently stated the record distance, which will be reached at 5:16:07 a.m. EST (101607 GMT) is "a huge milestone by any measure, and a day worth celebrating.".

In a recent development, during the light-day crossover, Voyager will be in contact with the Madrid station of the three-antenna Deep Space Network that monitors all deep-space missions. The spacecraft is presently making its way through the constellation Ophiuchus from the perspective of Earth, mentioned Jeffrey Hayes, a NASA official whose work includes Voyager 1.

In a recent development, "This [milestone] essentially kicks off the year's worth of celebrations leading up to the 50th anniversary in August and September of next year," added Hayes, who is discipline scientist in the agency's astrophysics and heliophysics divisions, in a livestreamed discussion with NASA's Night Sky Network on Nov. 4.

Voyager 1 is the farthest spacecraft from Earth, after launching from Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Sept. 5, 1977 a few weeks after its twin, Voyager 2.

Recent findings suggest that A light-day, as the name implies, represents the distance that light travels in a single day. In other words, at one light-day, a radio-wave message to Voyager 1 takes 24 hours to get to the spacecraft — which is roughly 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers) from Earth. Voyager's response then takes another day to get back to our planet.

Sources indicate that voyager 2 — which is at a distance of 13.5 billion miles (21.7 billion km) from our planet — won't hit the light-day milestone until 2035, NASA stated. While the agency has not offered recent estimates for how long the two spacecraft will last, in 2022 Suzanne Dodd, project manager for Voyager at JPL, said they may keep operating into the 2030s.

The two spacecraft had initial funding to survey Jupiter and Saturn, although NASA did launch them at a time when the planets aligned in such a way to bring Voyager 2 past Uranus and Neptune if funding continued — which it did.

Voyager 1, meanwhile, took a turn at Saturn to look at the planet's rings, and the pre-biotic (pre-life chemistry) moon of its largest moon Titan, executing maneuvers which brought it high above the solar system's plane.

Hayes stated the original design team likely did not foresee a 50-year lifespan for the mission, even though the Voyagers had many redundancies in them. But NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), which manages the mission, is looking to continue to max out the scientific return.

NASA says the mission costs from launch to Neptune, spanning about 12 years from 1977 to 1989, was $865 million — with $30 million more budgeted for its extended mission. "It's a lot of money, right? And it's everyone's money … so we want to make sure that we do it right," Hayes said.

Both nuclear-powered spacecraft are still healthy enough to be chatting with Earth and taking measurements from interstellar space, although dwindling power supplies have forced instrument shutoffs and other creative techniques to be getting the most out of the missions. One example was a huge power swap that took place on both spacecraft this year, called the "Major Bang" because of its impact on the mission.

Industry observers note that "It's a balance, right? Because some instruments are more power hungry than others," Hayes said of the ongoing work on keeping the Voyagers going. "Those instruments that use the least amount of power, but give you good science still, they would obviously rise to the top in any sort of priority discussion. Whereas an instrument that is more power-hungry, but still has interesting science, that's on the cusp.".

Sources indicate that while the two spacecraft are still healthy, Hayes mentioned their age — and the extreme environment they are operating in — makes them "fragile," in his words. "We're way out there. We're a light-day out there, which is just just over 16 billion miles. So it's really really far. It's also really really cold, right? We're only a few degrees above absolute zero here.".

The Voyagers continue to lose four watts of power per year (their initial power was at 470 watts apiece) and the challenge is not only the power, but also the propellant. Hydrazine, Hayes stated, is prone to freezing. "And if it freezes, then it's game over," he said, paying tribute to the JPL engineers that continue to keep the spacecraft going.

It has been revealed that voyager 1's next destination is vaguely near a star 17 light-years from our planet, in the constellation of Ursa Minor (the Little Bear, or Little Dipper). But the spacecraft will certainly be out of nuclear power by then, as its flyby — at a distance of 1.7 light-years of the star, called Gliese 445 — will take place in 40,000 years.

She was contributing writer for Space.com for 10 years from 2012 to 2024. Elizabeth's reporting includes multiple exclusives with the White House, leading world coverage about a lost-and-found space tomato on the International Space Station, witnessing five human spaceflight rolls out on two continents, flying parabolic, working inside a spacesuit, and participating in a simulated Mars mission. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Officials in South Sudan, the world’s youngest state, remarked on Saturday that its first national election would be postponed, raising new questions about a vote that analysts had already said could not yield a credible result.

Recent findings suggest that the National Elections Commission said in a statement that the presidential and legislative elections, which had been scheduled for Dec. 22, would be held on Feb. 11 instead. The country’s information minister, Ateny Wek Ateny, said the postponement would allow more time to register voters and educate them about the process.

Sources indicate that south Sudan has never held a national election. Since gaining independence from Sudan in 2011 after decades of war, it has been ruled by President Salva Kiir, and it has faced seemingly intractable political difficulties.

It has been revealed that in 2013, civil war broke out between the government and forces loyal to the main opposition leader, Riek Machar. Under a peace agreement to end the conflict in 2018, Mr. Machar became the vice president in a transitional government.

The upcoming election was supposed to underwrite that agreement. But the peace deal has unraveled since March 2025, when Mr. Machar was placed under house arrest in the capital, Juba, and charged with treason. In recent months, the government has replaced opposition lawmakers with its own supporters and dissolved the unity government.

It has been revealed that with Mr. Machar effectively sidelined, there are no credible challengers to Mr. Kiir, who is widely expected to win the presidential election. He has a broad national following, and his party controls state institutions and the news media.

The election faces stark logistical challenges. Civil servants have not been paid in more than a year, and parts of the country are controlled by armed groups, including Mr. Machar’s forces. Thousands of people have died in fighting and attacks on civilians. In March, more than 200 people were killed in a massacre in Unity State near the border with Sudan, according to human rights groups.

“The conditions for credible polls are not at the moment in place,” the International Crisis Group said in a briefing for the U.N. Security Council this week. “Rushed elections could be a decisive final blow to the 2018 framework and would open the door to a return to sustained large-scale violence.”.

Mr. Ateny, the information minister, acknowledged that the government could not gain access to “small parts” of the country, but said the election would be credible.

“It’s not always 100 percent, but it can be good for the sovereignty of the country and it’s good for the mandate of the state,” he stated in an interview.

Recent findings suggest that in addition to the violence and civil unrest, South Sudanese have been faced with soaring food prices, drought and flooding. Of the country’s roughly 12 million people, more than 8 million are in need of food assistance, according to the Famine Early Warning Systems Network, a globally recognized monitor of hunger.

Matthew Mpoke Bigg is the East Africa bureau chief for The New York Times, based in Nairobi, Kenya.

#12839. Scientists discover a hidden danger of viral infections that vaccines may prevent
